question: What did you say in your first address at the Parliament of Religions in Chicago?

result.text: As I told the audience at Chicago, it fills my heart with joy unspeakable to rise in response to the warm and cordial welcome which you have given us.[1] I thanked them in the name of the most ancient order of monks in the world; I thanked them in the name of the mother of religions; and I thanked them in the name of millions and millions of Hindu people of all classes and sects.[1] I wrote to Alasinga from Yokohama that the Parliament of Religions at Chicago was an opportunity for Hinduism to be properly represented and expounded to the American nation and the Western world.[2] I argued that the Parliament of Religions proved that Truth and Holiness are not the exclusive possessions of any particular locality or body of men or system of doctrine and discipline.[2] I emphasized that the whole world of religions is only a travelling, a coming up of different men and women through various conditions and circumstances to the same goal.[2] I stated that the recent Parliament of Religions at Chicago proved, to that date, that universal religion was impossible.[3]

question: How did your view of Buddhism relate to Hinduism in your Chicago addresses?

result.text: As I spoke at the Parliament of Religions in Chicago, I stated that I am not a Buddhist, yet I am, as I worship the Great Master as God incarnate on earth.[1] I explained that the relation between Hinduism and modern Buddhism is similar to that between Judaism and Christianity, with Buddha being the fulfilment of Hindu teachings, much like Jesus was for Judaism.[1] I argued that the separation between Buddhists and Brahmins has led to the downfall of India, and that the union of their intellect and heart is essential for its revival.[2] I emphasized that Buddhism and Hinduism are deeply connected, with Buddhism being a development and fulfilment of Hinduism, not a separate religion.[1] I noted that present-day Hinduism and Buddhism grew from the same branch, but Buddhism degenerated, while Hinduism, through thinkers like Shankara, corrected its course.[3] I pointed out that Buddhism taught 'Realise all this as illusion,' whereas Hinduism taught 'Realise that within the illusion is the Real,' allowing for a more flexible path to the divine.[4]

question: What did you write to Alasinga about starting work in Madras?

result.text: I wrote to Alasinga from New York that I had Rs. 9,000 with me, part of which I would send to him for the organisation, and I would get many people to send money to him in Madras yearly, half-yearly, or monthly.[1] I instructed Alasinga to start a Society and a journal and the necessary apparatus, and to collect funds from Mysore and elsewhere to build a temple in Madras which should have a library and some rooms for the office and the preachers who should be Sannyâsins, and for Vairâgis who may chance to come.[1] I told Alasinga that this was a great field for my work, and everything done there prepared the way for my coming work in England.[1] I wrote to Alasinga from the Oriental Hotel that I had a resolution in mind that would express the entire satisfaction of the Hindu community of Madras in my work.[2] I mentioned to Alasinga that I had done a good deal of work this year and hoped to do more in the next, and that my ideas were going to work in the West better than in India.[3] I told Alasinga that I had done more for India than India ever did for me, and that I believed in truth, the Lord sending me workers by the scores wherever I went.[3]

question: What did you say about the condition of the masses in India?

result.text: As I told the audience at Chicago, the poverty of the majority of the masses in India was strongly dwelt upon, with many earning less than fifty cents per month.[1] In my lecture, I pointed out that India is an enslaved race, with three hundred millions of people living in starvation and with no say in their own government.[2] During a dialogue, I spoke of the terrible famine in Central India and the death-roll of nine lakhs of starved people, asking if any help had been rendered to the suffering masses.[3] I argued that the great national sin is the neglect of the masses, and that until they are well educated, fed, and cared for, no amount of politics would be of any avail.[4] I described how the masses in India are practically our slaves, paying for our education and building our temples, but in return receiving only kicks.[5] I emphasized that the crying problem in India is poverty, and that young sannyasins must be trained both as secular and spiritual teachers and workers for the masses.[6]

question: What was your position on the caste system?

result.text: I argued at the 20th Century Club of Boston that the caste system is a social custom, not a religious institution, and that it is the outgrowth of political institutions in India.[1] In my lecture on India, I stated that the caste system is a hereditary trade guild, not a religious institution, and that it has existed from time immemorial.[2] I explained in a lecture that caste, as it relates to blood and heredity, has a role in preserving the purity of a race, though I acknowledged that this does not justify inequality.[3] In a discussion on caste, I noted that while it has its drawbacks, it also has benefits, such as uniting members of a caste and providing mutual support.[4] I wrote to Shrimati Mrinalini Bose that the caste system and other social customs are complex and require careful consideration.[5] In an interview, I stated that caste is a very good thing and that it is the plan we want to follow, as it has helped elevate many classes in India.[6] In a poem, I spoke of the importance of Jati Dharma, or hereditary caste system, as a path to welfare and freedom, though I warned against its misuse by the higher castes.[7]

question: What did you say about the education of women in India?

result.text: As I told the audience at Chicago, women must be put in a position to solve their own problems in their own way.[1] I argued that the education of women in India must be rooted in the spirit of their own religious ordinances, not in the Western style.[2] In my lecture on Women of India, I noted that Calcutta University opened its doors to women more than twenty years ago, and they graduated with the same standard as the boys.[3] I emphasized that the uplift of women and the awakening of the masses must come first for any real progress in the country.[4] I stated that the education of women in India depends on the men, and where men are highly cultured, women are also.[5] I warned that female education without a religious basis would lead to defects, and that religion must be the center of such education.[6]

question: How did you describe your Master, Shri Ramakrishna, in your lectures?

result.text: I spoke of Shri Ramakrishna's life as a living illustration of the ideas he preached.[1] I mentioned that his life was interesting and perhaps a little romantic for those in the West.[1] I described him as a force, not merely a teacher with a fixed doctrine, but a power still living in his disciples and working in the world.[2] I noted that he was both a Jivanmukta and an Acharya, indicating his spiritual realization and his role as a spiritual teacher.[2] I emphasized that his ideas were still growing and that he continued to influence the world through his disciples.[2] I also spoke of his deep connection with his disciples, such as Nag Mahashaya, who brought radiance to Eastern Bengal.[3] I acknowledged the diverse ways in which householder devotees preached about him, though I did not comment on their accuracy.[4]

question: What did you tell the people of Madras when you returned from the West?

result.text: As I told the audience at Madras during my return from the West, our object in approaching you with this address was not the performance of any merely formal or ceremonial function; we came to offer you the love of our hearts and to give expression to our feeling of thankfulness for the services you rendered to the cause of Truth by proclaiming India's lofty religious ideals.[1] I wrote to Miss Mary Hale that a late speech by the President of the Madras Christian College, Mr. Miller, embodied a large amount of my ideas and declared that the West is in need of Hindu ideas of God and man, calling upon the young men to go and preach to the West.[2] There I argued that the reception Niveditâ had in Madras was for the good of both Niveditâ and Madras, and her speech was indeed beautiful.[3] I mentioned that the Hindu public of Madras had been most eagerly expecting my arrival, and my name was on everybody's lips in the city, from the school to the streets and bazars.[4] I told the people of Madras that my mission was essentially spiritual, and I believed that India, the motherland of spirituality, had a great future before her, and the West would come to appreciate the sublime truths of Vedanta.[4] I also told them that my great motto was 'Help, and not Fight', 'Assimilation, and not Destruction', 'Harmony and Peace, and not Dissension'.[4]

question: What did you say about idol worship when questioned in the West?

result.text: I told the audience at the Parliament of Religions that external worship is the lowest stage of religious development, but it is a necessary stage for those who have not yet purified their inner self.[1] I explained that even though idol worship may seem primitive, it is not a sin, and those who practice it are in a stage of growth that should be respected and supported.[2] I argued that idol worship is a Pratika, a means of approaching God, and that it is not wrong to use such symbols as long as one does not mistake the idol for God Himself.[3] I pointed out that in the West, people often criticize idol worship without understanding that their own traditions also use symbolic representations of the divine, such as the ark in Jewish temples or the image of Jesus in Christian worship.[2] I criticized the Western tendency to condemn idol worship without recognizing the value of such practices in spiritual development, and I called out the hypocrisy of those who claim to have God but fail to live by His teachings.[4] I emphasized that the true worship of God is not in the idol itself, but in seeing God within the idol, and that one must eventually move beyond the idol to realize the divine directly.[3] I acknowledged that idol worship is a part of many religions, including Christianity and Judaism, and that it is not wrong to use such symbols as long as one does not become attached to them.[2] I warned against thinking that worshipping an idol or any other symbol will save a person, as one must ultimately seek God directly and not rely on external forms.[3]

question: What did you write about the relationship between science and religion?

result.text: I wrote that science is nothing but the finding of unity, and when it reaches perfect unity, it stops from further progress because it would reach the goal.[1] I argued that the fight between science and religion arises because religions are encumbered with explanations involving external spirits, whereas science seeks the cause of a thing within the nature of the thing itself.[2] I stated that all science ends where it finds a unity, and religion is no different, as the grand principle of religion was already mapped out when man discovered the Vedas' final words — 'I am He' — indicating the One in whom the universe finds its unity.[3] I explained that religion, like science, has its own methods, and the science of religion is based on the analysis of the human soul, with no creed.[4] I emphasized that experience is the only source of knowledge, and religion, when taught as a science of experience, becomes the real science of religion, with mystics across all religions speaking the same truth.[5] I noted that religion belongs to the supersensuous and not to the sense plane, being a vision, an inspiration, and a plunge into the unknown, making the unknowable more than known.[6]

question: What did you say about Christ in your lecture 'Christ, the Messenger'?

result.text: I spoke about Christ as a Messenger whose message was 'Be ready, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand.'[1] I explained that the life of Christ embodies the life of the past, shaped by heredity, surroundings, education, and reincarnation.[2] I emphasized that we should find God not only in Jesus of Nazareth but in all great Messengers who are manifestations of the same Infinite God.[3] I argued that it is not wrong to worship these great Messengers as God, since their characters exceed our conceptions of the divine.[4] I noted that the state of the Jews before Christ's birth was one of conservatism and stagnation, which made the rise of Jesus possible.[5] I stated that each Prophet and Messenger has a particular message, and their lives reflect that message in a radiant way.[6] I compared the march of events to waves on the ocean, with rises and falls being necessary for progress.[7] I wrote that all manifest life, including progress, moves in waves of activity and repose, successively.[8]

question: What did you say about Mohammedanism and Islam?

result.text: As I spoke at the 20th Century Club of Boston, I noted that the Vedantic spirit of religious liberality has significantly influenced Mohammedanism, especially in India, where it differs from Mohammedanism in other countries.[1] In my letter to Sarfaraz Husain, I stated that if any religion has approached equality in an appreciable manner, it is Islam and Islam alone.[2] I emphasized that the essential part of the Mohammedan religion is the practical brotherhood of all its followers, regardless of their background, which is a peculiar excellence of Mohammedanism.[3] In my lecture on Mohammed, I explained that Mohammedanism came as a message for the masses, with the first message being equality and the call to believe in one God, the creator of heaven and earth.[4] I also pointed out that some Mohammedans are the crudest in terms of sectarianism, with a watchword of exclusivity, but among them, philosophic individuals often protested against such cruelties, showing a touch of the Divine.[5] In my lecture on the realization of a universal religion, I argued that the heart of every religion, including Mohammedanism, remains sound and alive despite its mistakes and incrustations of forms.[3] I acknowledged that the question of whether Vedanta exerted any influence over Mohammedanism was raised, and I affirmed that it has indeed had an impact, particularly in India.[6] I suggested that for the motherland, a junction of Hinduism and Islam — Vedanta brain and Islam body — is the only hope for progress and unity.[7]

question: What were your views on the Vedas and their authority?

result.text: As I explained in my lecture on Vedantism, the Vedas are not the utterance of any person, but are eternal and self-authoritative, existing without beginning or end.[1] I emphasized that the Vedas are the knowledge of God, and their authority does not come from any personal being, but from their own eternal nature.[1] In my dialogue with Sharatchandra Chakravarty, I acknowledged that the Vedas are the highest authority for the theory of the Âtman, and nowhere else is it better established.[2] I wrote to Pramadadas Mitra that the Vedanta-Sutras do not provide a foundation for the authority of the Vedas, and that the argument that the Vedas are the breath of God may be circular.[3] In a poem, I stated that the authority of the Vedas extends to all ages, climes, and persons, and that their application is not confined to any particular place or time.[4] I noted that the Vedas are the only capable authority in matters of religious duty, and that other Shâstras are only to be accepted so far as they do not contradict the Vedas.[5] In my lecture on the Vedanta in all its phases, I stated that the philosophy of the Upanishads has been the first and final thought on the spiritual plane, with no certain date of origin.[6]

question: What did you say about the Sikhs and Guru Govind Singh?

result.text: I spoke about Guru Govind Singh during a conversation with Sharatchandra Chakravarty at Baghbazar, highlighting his role in reviving the Sikh sect through renunciation, austerities, and fortitude.[1] I noted that Guru Govind Singh united both Hindus and Mussulmans within the fold of his religion, leading them toward the same end, a rare example in Indian history.[2] I emphasized that Guru Govind Singh did not create a common interest but pointed out the injustice and oppression faced by both Hindus and Mussulmans, which led them to follow him.[3] I praised Guru Govind Singh as a great example of love and forgiveness, even when deserted by those for whom he had shed his blood, and called for all to emulate his ideal.[4] I recited a popular Dohâ of the Sikhs, illustrating the great power infused into the initiates of Guru Govind, and how his life was marked by heroism and spiritual devotion.[5] I mentioned Guru Govind Singh as a great worshipper of Shakti, and noted that such an example is indeed very rare in Indian history.[3] I described Guru Govind Singh as a wounded lion who retired to die in the South, without a word of curse against those who had forsaken him, embodying the ideal of a true Hindu.[6]

question: What did you write to Sister Nivedita about her work for Indian women?

result.text: I wrote to Sister Nivedita from Darjeeling in 1897, telling her I had found important work for her to do on behalf of the downtrodden masses of India.[1] I wrote to Sister Nivedita from The Math in 1901, expressing my gladness about the good work she was doing in England and joining in prayer for her future services to India by her pen.[2] I wrote to Sister Nivedita from Gopal Lal Villa in 1902, instructing her to open letters for me if I passed away and to take care of Christina Greenstidel, who was traveling to India.[3] I wrote to Sister Nivedita from The Math in 1901, mentioning that Yum had spoken with Mother about her and that Mother had desired her to come over, though it was out of love and anxiety.[2]

question: What did you say about vegetarianism and meat-eating?

result.text: I wrote in The Education That India Needs that my Master was a vegetarian, but if he was given meat offered to the Goddess, he used to hold it up to his head[1] I argued in The East and the West that while vegetarianism is purer, those who must live a strenuous life in the world must take meat[2] I noted in a newspaper report that vegetarianism began in India, but the belief that Hindus avoid meat to avoid eating ancestors is false[3] I stated in a lecture that eating meat is not inherently sinful, but that forcing vegetarianism on those who labor is harmful to national freedom[1] I said in The Women of India that while men may eat meat, women of higher caste do not, showing their adherence to religious law[4] I declared in Sayings and Utterances that I teach meat-eating in India to build a militant spirit[5] I wrote in The East and the West that the strongest nations are those that take animal food, and that vegetarians cannot be expected to perform the same feats of labor[6] I explained in a dialogue that eating meat is not necessarily improper, and that some Hindu men do eat meat[4]

question: What was your opinion of social reformers in India?

result.text: I wrote in The Social Conference Address that the social reformers in India have not produced any permanent and valuable result appreciable throughout the country.[1] I stated that most of the social reformers are good, well-meaning men with laudable aims, but their efforts have not led to practical change.[1] I argued that many modern reform movements in India have been inconsiderate imitations of Western methods, which will not work for India.[1] I emphasized that the reason for the lack of success in social reform is the denunciation of Hindu civilization, which has not led to any good practical result.[1] I pointed out that the true reformers in history, such as Shankara and Chaitanya, were constructive and built according to the circumstances of their time.[2] I noted that the modern reformers often take to European destructive reformation, which will never do good to anyone.[2] I acknowledged that Raja Ram Mohan Ray was the only modern reformer who was mostly constructive.[2]

question: What did you say about the Theosophists?

result.text: I wrote to Alasinga from Yokohama that any suspicion of my connection with the Theosophists would spoil my work both in America and England.[1] I told the audience at Colombo that the Theosophists have not much power, but they are dead set against the orthodox section.[2] I argued in an essay that the Theosophists wanted to crawl into the heart of Western Society, catching on to the skirts of scholars like Max Müller and poets like Edwin Arnold, all the same denouncing these very men.[3] I said in a lecture that the Theosophists have done some good work for India, and especially Mrs. Besant deserves gratitude for her efforts to raise our country.[4] I remarked in a letter that in India, Theosophists and Buddhists are nonentities, publishing a few papers and making a lot of splash to catch Occidental ears.[5] I wrote in an essay that the Theosophists prepared the way for my success, but I called it pure nonsense.[6] I noted in an essay that the Theosophists' help to Hindu religion in the West was not a ready field, but years of uphill work, necessitated by Theosophical sleight-of-hand methods.[3]

question: What did you say about the English and British rule in India?

result.text: I wrote to Miss Mary Hale from Ridgely Manor on 1899-10-30 that British rule in modern India has only one redeeming feature, though unconscious; it has brought India out once more on the stage of the world; it has forced upon it the contact of the outside world.[1] I wrote to Miss Mary Hale from Ridgely Manor on 1899-10-30 that if it had been done with an eye to the good of the people concerned, as circumstances favoured Japan with, the results could have been more wonderful for India.[1] I wrote to Miss Mary Hale from Ridgely Manor on 1899-10-30 that there has been a good increase of population, but not yet what it was when the country was entirely independent — that is, before the Mohammedan rule.[2] I told the audience at the Pouch mansion that the English used three B's — Bible, brandy and bayonets — in civilizing India.[3] One consisting of those who hate everything Indian, but they are uneducated.[4] And they try to out-Herod Herod in their Hinduism.[4] I wrote in a translation of prose from Vol 4, Modern India that the English are trying to maintain their supremacy in India by keeping uppermost in the heart of every Indian the mighty prestige and glory of the British nation.[5] I wrote in a translation of prose from Vol 4, Modern India that so long as these qualities are inherent in the British character, let thousands of such Indian Empires be lost, thousands will be earned again.[5]

question: What did you write about the historical evolution of India?

result.text: I wrote about the historical evolution of India, noting that the ancient history of India is full of descriptions of the gigantic energies and their multifarious workings, the boundless spirit, and the profound thoughtfulness of a godly race.[1] I wrote that the civilisations of Egypt and ancient Babylonia are the oldest, but India has books of a far earlier date, with evidence showing that the Vedas of the Hindus existed in the present form at least five thousand years before the Christian era.[2] I wrote that the commerce of India has been one of the most important causes for the present state of human civilisation, as India has long supplied the world with commodities such as cotton, jute, indigo, and spices.[3] I wrote that Indian philosophy, coming in contact with Greek energy, led to the rise of the Persian, the Roman, and other great nations, and that such a conjunction of forces may again present itself with India as the centre.[4] I wrote that the Vedas are the common source of Hinduism in all its varied stages, as also of Buddhism and every other religious belief in India, with the seeds of Indian thought on religion lying buried in the Vedas.[5] I wrote that the northern reaction of ritualism was followed by the fitful glory of the Malava empire, and that the south was the home of refuge of Indian religion and civilisation when northern India was under Central Asiatic conquerors.[6] I wrote that non-existence can never be the cause of what exists, and that the law of causation is omnipotent and knows no time or place when it did not exist, a doctrine as old as the Aryan race.[7]

question: How did you describe the Sannyasin's ideal in your poem?

result.text: In my poem, I described the Sannyasin as having no home, with the sky as their roof and the grass as their bed.[1] I wrote that the Sannyasin should accept whatever food or drink comes their way, without judgment.[1] I portrayed the Sannyasin as free like a rolling river, ever moving and unbound.[1] I called upon the Sannyasin to embody the truth of 'Om Tat Sat, Om,' affirming their spiritual identity.[1]

question: What did you say to your brother disciples about organising the Ramakrishna Mission?

result.text: I wrote to the brother-disciples at Alambazar Monastery that I was giving them a new idea, and if they could work it out, then I would know they were men and would be of service.[1] I told them to make an organised plan, including getting a big hut, some cameras, maps, globes, and chemicals, and to teach poor and indigent folk through pictures and oral teaching.[1] I asked them if they could send out lady devotees to convert widows into disciples and then send them out to preach Sri Ramakrishna from door to door, along with imparting education.[2] I urged them to go to the cottages of the poor and open their eyes to the world through teaching, rather than relying on books.[1] I mentioned that the Society of Shri Ramakrishna was named the Ramakrishna Mission after discussion with householder disciples.[3] I expressed my hope that the Ramakrishna Mission would take a significant part in the regenerating work of India.[4]

question: What did you say about Shankaracharya and Advaita?

result.text: I discussed Shankaracharya's Advaita philosophy in a dialogue with a disciple who was a great adherent of Shankara, almost to the point of fanaticism.[1] I explained that the Advaita philosophy, as understood in the Upanishads, is a progression of steps leading to the final realization of Advaitism, with 'Tattvamasi' being the last step.[2] I pointed out that Shankaracharya, along with Râmânujâchârya and Madhvâchârya, had committed mistakes by twisting passages in the Upanishads to support their own theories.[2] I noted that Shankaracharya's influence was immense in Southern India, where the Smârtas are all followers of Shankaracharya, and his teachings have been the great preachers of Advaita both in Southern and Northern India.[3] I stated that Shankaracharya arose to revivify the Vedanta philosophy and made it a rationalistic philosophy, emphasizing the intellectual side of the teachings.[4] I acknowledged that Shankaracharya, through his realisation of Oneness, said, 'Where is the universe vanished?', aligning with the Advaita philosophy's understanding of the Absolute.[5]

question: What did you say about Ramanuja and qualified non-dualism?

result.text: I explained that Ramanuja's system admits the unity of the total, but within that totality, there are eternal differences.[1] I noted that for all practical purposes, Ramanuja's system is dualistic, making it easy to keep the distinction between the personal soul and the Personal God clear.[1] I described how the qualified non-dualists believe the soul and nature are simply the expansion or body of God, just as the body of man is to man's soul.[2] I stated that the qualified non-dualists claim the effect is never different from the cause, and as God is the cause of the universe, he is also the effect.[2] I mentioned that the souls are all parts of God, and that God is interpenetrating everything in the universe, not that God has become the wall, but that God is in the wall.[3] I explained that according to Ramanuja, the souls are eternal and will remain individualised through eternity, and will retain their individuality all through.[4] I noted that Ramanuja is the leading dualistic philosopher of later India, and that all other dualistic sects have followed him, directly or indirectly.[5]

question: What did you say about the Buddha as a person?

result.text: I spoke highly of Buddha's character, saying he stood head and shoulders above all other men, and that his friends or enemies could never say he drew a breath or ate a crumb of bread but for the good of all.[1][2] I expressed deep veneration for Buddha, noting his boldness, fearlessness, and tremendous love, and how he lived solely for the good of others, never seeking truth for himself but for the relief of human misery.[3] I emphasized that Buddha's message was one of complete unselfishness, urging people to root out selfishness and detach from worldly attachments like family and possessions.[4] I recounted how Buddha, even in death, showed great compassion and detachment, telling his disciples that he had been released from the body by the food offered to him by a member of a race similar to the American Indians.[5] I noted that Buddha was more brave and sincere than any teacher, rejecting the Vedas as humbug and declaring himself the greatest book, emphasizing that morality must be practiced for its own sake.[6] I pointed out that Buddha did not believe in God, and that his teachings focused on the power within man himself, arguing that God helps those who work hard and that dependence weakens the spirit.[7] I described Buddha as a man who reached the highest state of perfection without belief in God, showing that perfection comes through disinterested action, not faith or doctrine.[8]

question: What did you say about the role of the Brahmin in India's future?

result.text: I argued that the Brahmin must work for the salvation of the rest of mankind in India, and that he is a true Brahmin only when he does so, not when he pursues secular employment.[1] I stated that the accumulated culture of ages, which the Brahmin has been the trustee of, must now be given to the people at large, and that it was because he did not do so that the Mohammedan invasion was possible.[2] I emphasized that the solution of the caste problem in India is not to degrade the higher castes or crush out the Brahmin, but to uphold the ideal of Brahminhood as the ideal of humanity in India.[3] I pointed out that the Brahmin must open the treasury of virtue and distribute its valuables to the world, and that he must be the first to do so in order to break open the cells that hide the treasures accumulated by our common ancestors.[2] I noted that the Brahmin must not use his power for evil, but only for good, and that the days of exclusive privileges and claims are gone forever from the soil of India.[3] I mentioned that the Brahmin, as the ideal of the Hindu race, must be spiritual, moral, and good, and that the ideal of caste is meant for raising all humanity towards the realisation of the spiritual man.[4] I warned that the Brahmin, if he does not give the culture he has accumulated to the people, will continue to suffer the consequences of neglect, and that the non-Brahmin castes must also take responsibility for their own neglect of spirituality and Sanskrit learning.[2] I acknowledged that the Brahmin has been the earliest preacher to the Indian races and the first to renounce everything for the higher realisation of life, but that the other castes have failed to follow his example.[1]

question: What did you say about Japan when you visited it?

result.text: I wrote to Mr. Okakura Kakuzo from The Math on 1901-06-18 that Japan to me is a dream — so beautiful that it haunts one all his life.[1] I told the audience at The Abroad and the Problems at Home that the world has never seen such a patriotic and artistic race as the Japanese, and one special feature about them is this that while in Europe and elsewhere Art generally goes with dirt, Japanese Art is Art plus absolute cleanliness.[2] I argued with Shri Priya Nath Sinha that in Japan, you find a fine assimilation of knowledge, and not its indigestion, as we have here.[3] I wrote to Miss Josephine MacLeod from The Math on 1901-06-14 that we will have to learn many things from Japan, and that the help that Japan will give us will be with great sympathy and respect.[4] I mentioned in an interview that I would wish that every one of our young men could visit Japan once at least in his lifetime.[2] I expressed in a letter to Sister Christine from The Math on 1901-09-25 that I am just thinking of going over to Japan, as Miss [Josephine] MacLeod is so insistent.[5]

question: What did you say about American women?

result.text: As I told the audience at Chicago, I have a good impression of this country especially of the American women.[1] There I argued that in America the women are more learned than men, and they are all well versed in science and philosophy.[2] I wrote to Alasinga from Chicago that the average American woman is far more cultivated than the average American man.[3] I also mentioned that the American women are intellectual, but they are not steady, serious and sincere, according to my observations.[4] In a letter to my disciples in Madras, I expressed my gratitude for the kindness of American women, who are the life of every movement in this country.[5] I noted that American women are more advanced than men, as the men are too busy with work, while the women seize every opportunity to improve themselves.[3] I also remarked that in America, the women are entering the medical profession to some extent and that I see no reason why they should not vote.[6] I praised the American women most enthusiastically, as reported in a newspaper from Chicago.[7]

question: What did you say about the Jains?

result.text: I spoke about the Jains in a lecture, noting that they are an ancient sect in India who challenged the validity of the Hindu scriptures, the Vedas, and claimed that their own writings were the original Vedas.[1] I mentioned that the Jains are known for their remarkable kindness to dumb animals, and their moral law is summed up in the principle of not injuring others.[2] I described the Jains as ascetics who emphasized the principle of non-injury and doing good to all, and argued that the Brahmins created much of the moral and ethical framework that followed.[3] I noted that the Jains, like the Buddhists, do not depend upon God, but their religion is directed toward evolving a God out of man, having seen the Son rather than the Father.[4] I wrote that the doctrine of the eternity of creation is a corner-stone not only of the Hindu religion, but also of the Buddhists and Jains.[5] I described the Jains as a sect that believes in the soul but not in the moral government of the country, and noted that their priests and monks tie a handkerchief over their faces to avoid harming others with their breath.[6]

question: What did you write about the Paris Congress of the History of Religions?

result.text: I wrote that the Paris Congress of the History of Religions was similar to the Congress of Orientalists, but with the addition of the antiquarianism of Christianity.[1] I wrote that the Paris Congress focused only on the historic evolution of religions and excluded the representation of missionary sects and their beliefs.[2] I wrote that the Chicago Parliament of Religions was a grand affair with many religious representatives, unlike the Paris Congress, which was attended only by scholars studying the history of religions.[2] I wrote that the Roman Catholics were the organizers of the Chicago Parliament and hoped to establish their superiority over Protestants, but the result was disappointing.[2] I wrote that the Paris Congress was not a big affair and that only a few scholars discussed topics like the origin of the Shâlagrâma and Jehovah.[3] I wrote that I was invited to the Paris Congress to contradict certain convictions but was unable to keep my promise due to ill health.[4] I wrote that I was warmly received by Western Sanskrit scholars at the Paris Congress, who admired my lectures on Vedanta.[4] I wrote that the substance of my lecture at the Paris Congress would be printed in the General Report of the Congress in French.[5] I wrote that the Parliament of Religions in Chicago was a tremendous success for India and Indian thought, helping to spread Vedanta globally.[6]

question: What did you say about the Vedanta being practical?

result.text: As I told the audience at the lecture on Practical Vedanta, theory is very good, but how we carry it into practice is what truly matters.[1] I argued that the Vedanta must be intensely practical, and that the fictitious differentiation between religion and the life of the world must vanish, for the Vedanta teaches oneness — one life throughout.[1] I explained that the Vedanta teaches that the ideal is always far ahead of the real, but that it is not impractical, as it is always in the sense of the ideal.[2] I stated that the Vedanta teaches that not only can this ideal be realised in the depths of forests or caves, but by men in all possible conditions of life, even by those who led the busiest of lives.[3] I mentioned that the Vedanta must be able to help man wherever he may be, in servitude or in freedom, in the depths of degradation or on the heights of purity, everywhere, equally.[4] I said that the goal of the Vedanta is intense activity, but in the midst of it, eternal calmness, and that inactivity cannot be the goal of the Vedanta.[5] I told the audience that the plan of Vedanta is first to lay down the principles, map out for us the goal, and then to teach us the method by which to arrive at the goal.[6]

question: What did you say about Kali and Mother worship?

result.text: I wrote to Swami Brahmananda from the U.S.A. on 1899-11-20 that I bless you all and that the Mother will certainly come down with great strength to bring all victory.[1] I told Sharat Chandra Chakravarty that in the figure of Mother Kali there is the union of the blissful and the terrible aspects, but these are not adequately expressed in pictures.[2] I sang a song of Kali, saying, 'O Mother, Thou flowing stream of nectar, in how many forms and aspects dost Thou play in manifestation!'[3] I mentioned that Kali is Brahman in manifestation and referred to Shri Ramakrishna's illustration of the 'snake moving and the snake at rest'.[3] I stated that Kali worship is my special fad, but I never preached it in India or explained it to anyone, as it is not necessary for any religion.[4] I spoke of the worship of even one spark of Mother in our earthly mother leading to greatness and emphasized the importance of worshiping Her for love.[5]

question: What did you say about the hymn 'As the different streams having their sources in different places'?

result.text: As I told the audience at the Parliament of Religions, I quoted a hymn which every Hindoo child repeats every day, emphasizing that the spirit of this hymn has at last come to be realized.[1] I mentioned that this hymn, which I remember repeating from my earliest boyhood, is every day repeated by millions of human beings.[1] I used the hymn to illustrate the idea that different paths, though various and crooked or straight, all lead to the same destination.[1] I explained that the hymn reflects the belief that all religions are true and that different sects are but different manifestations of religion.[2] I emphasized that the hymn is not merely a theory but a profound recognition of the unity underlying all religious paths.[2] I noted that the hymn is a powerful expression of the unity in variety that characterizes the universe.[3] I stated that hymns, like this one, are not only words of praise but also words of power when pronounced with the right attitude of mind.[4]

question: What did you say about the Gita and Krishna's historicity?

result.text: As I discussed in my lectures on the Gita, it is important to consider whether the Gita formed a part of the Mahabharata and whether Krishna was a historical figure.[1] I noted that Krishna was likely a king, as it was common for kings in ancient times to promote the teachings of Brahma-Jnâna.[2] I mentioned that the Gita may have been the scripture of a sect that embodied its ideas in this sacred book, and that its teachings align with those of the Mahabharata.[2] I described Krishna as a figure who lived five thousand years ago, with a life full of miracles similar to those of Christ, and who was born in prison.[3] I expressed doubt about whether Krishna ever lived, stating that many stories are told of him but I do not believe them.[4] I acknowledged that the personality of Krishna has become so obscured that it is difficult to draw inspiration from his life today.[5] I often told my followers that Krishna, like Christ, was a figure whose historical existence was uncertain, and that many legends were woven around him.[6]

question: How did you define religion in your lectures?

result.text: As I explained in my lecture at Harris' Academy of Music Concert Hall, religion is the manifestation of the Divinity already in man.[1] I stated in my lecture on 'What Is Religion?' that religion is the realisation of Spirit as Spirit; not Spirit as matter.[2][3] In my lecture on 'What We Believe in,' I said that religion is the idea which is raising the brute unto man, and man unto God.[4][5] I argued in my lecture on 'The Necessity of Religion' that religion is the greatest motive power that moves the human mind.[6] I described religion as the realisation of the infinite, where one sees God in every person and feels oneness with the universe.[2] I taught that religion is not about destruction or breaking down, but about giving people something better and helping them grow.[7] I said that religion is not limited to any one faith, but is a universal truth that accepts all religions and their teachings.[8] I defined religion as the highest spiritual worship, where one realises that they are the universal and one with the Infinite.[2] I taught that religion is the voice of the centuries, coming from the sages and prophets of all nations, calling for peace and unity among all religions.[9]

question: What did you say about the problem of evil?

result.text: As I spoke at the lecture on Worshipper and Worshipped, I explained that the only way to solve the problem of evil is to accept that God is the cause of both good and evil.[1] I argued that denying the existence of evil is a weakness and that God has indeed placed evil in the world, but we must have faith and not try to whitewash Him.[2] At the Brooklyn Ethical Society, I was asked how I reconcile my optimistic views with the existence of evil, and I responded that the Vedantic religion does not admit the existence of evil as a permanent state.[3] I emphasized that good and evil are not separate existences but part of an evolution, and that what we call evil is simply a stage in the development of good.[4] In my lecture, I noted that evil is present everywhere and that sometimes good can become evil, just as evil can become good under certain conditions.[5] I described life as being accompanied by evil, and that a little evil is the source of life, contributing to the balance that eventually leads to the end of the world.[6]

question: What did you say about hypnotism and psychic powers?

result.text: I wrote in my notes on Raja-Yoga that the great danger of psychic powers is that man stumbles into them without training or knowledge of what has happened to him.[1] In my lecture on the Mundaka Upanishad, I argued that the idea of a man or woman in the soul is nonsense and a form of terrible hypnotism.[2] I was asked by a disciple about what I had personally seen of psychic powers, but I did not elaborate on my own experiences.[3] I explained that in the West, unusual mental powers are often looked upon as bordering on witchcraft and mysticism, and that the study of higher psychology has been hindered by this association.[4] In a discussion, I remarked that spiritual and psychic powers can be quickly developed through religious practice, as demonstrated by a letter from one of Swami Saradananda's disciples.[5] I spoke about how the atmosphere of a room can be hypnotised so that everyone who enters it will see all sorts of things, such as men and objects flying through the air.[6] In my lecture on the Mundaka Upanishad, I said that as long as one is under the hypnotism of duality, one will have to see God, nature, and the soul, but when one is beyond it, they will vanish.[7] I told a story in my lecture on the powers of the mind about a man who could answer questions and predict events, even writing down sentences in languages he did not know, which were later confirmed by the people who had them.[8]

question: What did you tell the Alambazar Math members about rules of the monastery?

result.text: I wrote to the members of the Alambazar Math that no Sannyasin shall be allowed to reside in the Women's Math, and anyone refusing to obey this rule shall be expelled from the Math.[1] I explained that it is necessary at the immature stage to be guided by rules, as the Master used to say that the sapling must be hedged round, and so on.[2] I warned that if any feeling of jealousy or egotism gain ground amongst you, it will be a great pity, and there is a danger of all our labours coming to naught.[2] I advised that if you follow the hints I jot down, you will undoubtedly prosper, but if you don't do so, then there is a danger of all our labours coming to naught.[2]

question: What did you say about Mahavira and Indian history?

result.text: I spoke about Mahâvira as an ideal of personal service and moral courage, emphasizing his perfect mastery of the senses and his unwavering devotion to Râmachandra.[1] I argued that Mahâvira's example, like that of Hanumân, represents leonine courage and whole-hearted devotion to the service of Rama, even at the cost of life itself.[1] I mentioned that Jainism represents the extreme of self-torture, while Chaitanyaism represents the other extreme of enjoyment, and that Buddhism is a reformed version of Jainism.[2] I noted that in Indian history, various religious movements such as Jainism, Buddhism, and Chaitanyaism have played significant roles in shaping society and countering the excesses of ritualistic practices.[3] I emphasized that the Jain revolution, with its focus on chaste morals and philosophical truth, helped save Indian society from the burden of ritualistic ceremonialism.[3] I pointed out that in every age, Indian history has seen cycles of religious and philosophical movements, from the extreme of self-torture to the extreme of excess, with metaphysical cycles complementing them.[2] I stated that the Jain movement, along with Buddhism and other reformist movements, has been crucial in addressing the social and spiritual needs of Indian society throughout history.[3]

question: What did you write about the East and the West in your essay?

result.text: I wrote that the East and the West have different ideals, with the West focusing on perfecting the social state and the East on perfecting the individual through Sannyasa and concentration.[1] I noted that the West is adroit in organised action, while the East is bold in searching for the mysteries of the internal world.[2] I observed that the West sees the universe as full of happiness, while the East views Samsara as full of misery and unreal.[2] I pointed out that in the West, ideas of decency and etiquette vary from country to country, unlike in the East.[3] I stated that both the East and the West have their own good, and neither can be praised or blamed more than the other.[4] I mentioned that the East also sends missionaries to England, just as the West sends them to India.[5]

question: What did you say about Sister Nivedita's book on Kali?

result.text: I discussed the figure of Mother Kali with Sister Nivedita, emphasizing the union of the blissful and the terrible aspects in her image.[1] I expressed the need for a proper artistic representation of Mother Kali that captures both her terrible and blissful aspects.[1] I shared some ideas about the terrible aspects of Mother Kali in my English poem, Kali the Mother, during a conversation with Sister Nivedita.[1] I encouraged Sister Nivedita to express these ideas in a picture, as I believed it would be a powerful way to convey the depth of Kali's symbolism.[1]

question: What did you say about the Arya Samaj and Dayananda?

result.text: I wrote to Akhandananda from London that I should teach against the marriage of boys, and I asked him to inquire about a Sannyasin named Achyutananda who used to live with the Arya Samaj.[1] I mentioned in a letter to Mr.__ from Almora that Swami Dayananda thought he could find a consistent theory of the whole based on a new interpretation of the Samhitas, but the difficulties remained the same.[2] In a letter to Miss Mary Hale from Ridgely Manor, I criticized the Arya Samaj and other sects as being useless mixtures, only voices of apology to our English masters.[3] I spoke of the Arya Samaj in a translation of Modern India, noting that it, along with the Brahmo Samaj, was part of a wave of religious change in India.[4] I was received in Lahore by the leaders of the Arya Samaj and the Sanâtana Dharma Sabhâ, and I delivered a lecture on 'The Common Bases of Hinduism' there.[5]

question: What did you say about Tantra and the Tantras?

result.text: I wrote in my lecture on the Religion We Are Born in that I have no faith in the theories advanced by Western savants with regard to the Vedas, as they keep changing the antiquity of the Vedas.[1] I stated that the Puranas are authoritative only in so far as they agree with the Vedas, otherwise not, and that the Tantras contain many high and sublime Vedantic thoughts.[1] I denounced only the present corrupted form of Vâmâchâra of the Tantras, not the Mother-worship or the real Vamachara, which is to worship women in a spirit of Divinity.[2] I explained that the Tantras represent the Vedic rituals in a modified form, and advised people to read the Tantras in conjunction with the Brahmanas, especially the Adhvaryu portion.[3] I mentioned that the Tântrika rites among the Tibetans arose in India during the decline of Buddhism, and were the creation of the Buddhists themselves.[4] I argued that modern Vaishnavism is saturated with Vamachara, which is contrary to the spirit of the Vedas, and that we must stem the tide of this Vamachara.[5] I noted that the Tantras, like the Puranas, contain many beautiful and illuminating teachings on Yoga, Bhakti, Jnâna, and Karma, which we should accept.[1] I stated that the real meaning of the word Tantra is Shâstra, and that the Brâhmana portions of the Vedas were modified and incorporated into the body of the Tantras.[1]

question: What did you say about spiritualism and talking to the dead?

result.text: I wrote to the editor of Light on July 11, 1896, that the truth of correspondence between the living and the dead is present in every religion, especially in the Vedantic sects of India.[1] I told the audience at a lecture that I have attended several spiritualistic meetings, and in one, the leader said that my mother and grandfather came to her, but my mother is still alive.[2] I said that I would be very sorry if my dead father is still wearing his filthy body, and that people get consolation from the idea that their fathers are encased in matter.[2] I mentioned that in another place, they brought me Jesus Christ, and I said, 'Lord, how do you do?' which makes me feel hopeless if that great saintly man is still wearing the body.[2] I wrote that I believe in the possibility of spirits communicating with mortals and that at times spirits of a high grade visit earth to assist mankind, but that the Vedanta Philosophy does not recommend seeking such intercourse due to its possible dangers.[3] I stated that I have witnessed some spiritualist cases, but they seemed to be a hoax, and I shall test some more before coming to a final conclusion.[4] I said that spiritualism is also a manifestation of Pranayama, and if it be true that the departed spirits exist, only we cannot see them, it is quite probable that there may be hundreds and millions of them about us we can neither see, feel, nor touch.[5]

question: What did you say about the poverty of your own family?

result.text: I wrote to Maharaja Ajit Singh that I have been trying to make Sevâ and serve my mother, for some years at least, and want to live with my mother and get my younger brother married to prevent extinction of the family.[1] I told Sister Nivedita that I have spent the little money I brought from Europe in feeding my mother and paying her debts.[2] I spoke of how my mother and brothers were left poor and almost starving all the time, and I was the only hope of the family.[3] I wrote to Your Highness that I have one great sin rankling always in my breast, and that is to do a service to the world, I have sadly neglected my mother.[1] I told the audience at My Life and Mission that my mother lives now in a hovel and I want to build a little, decent home for her.[1] I wrote to Your Highness that I want to make some provision for the youngest, as there is very little hope of his being a good earning man.[1]

question: What did you say about the Chicago Fair and your early days in America?

result.text: I wrote to Alasinga from Breezy Meadows that in Chicago, a funny thing happened involving the Raja of Kapurthala and some eccentric Mahratta Brâhmin selling pictures in the Fair.[1] I wrote to Alasinga from Breezy Meadows that I remained about twelve days in Chicago and almost every day I used to go to the Fair, which is a tremendous affair.[2] I told the audience at Chicago that the World's Parliament of Religions was held there at the time of the World's Fair, instead of in London, as it ought to have been.[3] I told the audience at Chicago that the Americans are a great people, with a future before them, and that they are less prejudiced than the English, more ready to weigh and examine a new idea.[3] I told the audience at Chicago that the substance of my exposition at the Parliament of Religions was a revelation to many of my audience, and its manner overpowering by its grace and strength.[4] I wrote to Alasinga from Breezy Meadows that in Chicago, the newspaper editors made capital out of me to give my countryman a brushing, showing that intellect carries more weight than all the pomp of money and title.[1] I told the audience at Chicago that my opportunities widened during my time there, and I had to meet call after call from many cities in many States, answer many queries, and satisfy many doubts.[4] I told the audience at Chicago that my teaching has deeply influenced many an enlightened circle in the American Commonwealth, has stimulated thought and research, and has in many instances definitely altered religious conceptions.[4]

question: What did you say about your health and illness in your last years?

result.text: I wrote to Alasinga from Yokohama that I was sorry to learn that you are not in perfect health, sure you will be in a few days.[1] I told Sister Christine that I was once more in the vale of death, with the old diabetes now replaced by asthma or dyspepsia due to nervous prostration, and that I was best in Calcutta for rest and quiet.[2] I wrote to Swami Ramakrishnananda that my illness was now much less, and may even be cured completely if the Lord wills.[3] I wrote to Miss Mary Hale that my health was getting worse every day, with many complications and botherations.[4] I spoke of my health in a dialogue, saying that my body was getting unfit for work day by day, and that some disease or other was always overtaking it.[5] I wrote to my brother-disciples that illness was due to their negative, self-abasing spirit, and that they should brush it aside by mental strength.[6] I wrote to Miss Josephine Macleod that I had had several attacks of fever, the last being influenza.[7] I told Miss Mary Hale that I had arrived and had received a letter from Isabelle, and that I was trying to write a book on India and her people.[8]

question: What did you say about music and art in India?

result.text: As I discussed in my lecture at Wendte Hall, San Francisco, India was the first to develop music with full seven notes, even to half and quarter notes, and led in music, drama, and sculpture.[1][2] I argued that the real music of India lies in Kirtana and Dhrupada, and that the introduction of Islamic methods, such as Tappa songs, has spoiled the science of music.[3] I noted that in ancient times, Indian drama was considered a holy thing, and that any song, if sung with one's whole soul, could lead to salvation.[4] I observed that in the West, art tends to be pointed and sharp, while in India, music and dance have a rolling, wave-like movement.[5] I explained that the introduction of Tappa songs led to the loss of the poetry and structure of Indian music, and that true art is slowly reviving with the improvement in theatres.[6] I remarked that the music of the Westerners is much advanced, with a sentiment of pathos and heroism, but our antique musical instruments have not been improved further.[7]

question: What is Karma-Yoga?

result.text:
Karma-Yoga is the knowledge of the secret of work, aimed at achieving salvation and liberty through understanding the purpose of work in the universe.
“What is Karma-Yoga? The knowledge of the secret of work. We see that the whole universe is working. For what? For salvation, for liberty; from the atom to the highest being, working for the one end, liberty for the mind, for the body, for the spirit. All things are always trying to get freedom, flying away from bondage. The sun, the moon, the earth, the planets, all are trying to fly away from bondage. The centrifugal and the centripetal forces of nature are indeed typical of our universe. Instead of being knocked about in this universe, and after long delay and thrashing, getting to know things as they are, we learn from Karma-Yoga the secret of work, the method of work, the organising power of work. A vast mass of energy may be spent in vain if we do not know how to utilise it. Karma-Yoga makes a science of work; you learn by it how best to utilise all the workings of this world. Work is inevitable, it must be so; but we should work to the highest purpose. Karma-Yoga makes us admit that this world is a world of five minutes, that it is a something we have to pass through; and that freedom is not here, but is only to be found beyond. To find the way out of the bondages of the world we have to go through it slowly and surely.” [1]

question: What is Raja-Yoga?

result.text:
Raja-Yoga is the psychological path to union, and it involves the method of concentration as the central idea.
“We take the Raja-Yoga, the psychological Yoga, the psychological way to union. It is a vast subject, and I can only point out to you now the central idea of this Yoga. We have but one method of acquiring knowledge.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Ch. 1: Introductory].

question: What is Bhakti-Yoga?

result.text:
Bhakti-Yoga is the science of higher love, showing us how to direct and manage it for spiritual blessedness.
“Bhakti-Yoga is the science of higher love. It shows us how to direct it; it shows us how to control it, how to manage it, how to use it, how to give it a new aim, as it were, and from it obtain the highest and most glorious results, that is, how to make it lead us to spiritual blessedness. Bhakti-Yoga does not say, "Give up"; it only says, "Love; love the Highest !" — and everything low naturally falls off from him, the object of whose love is the Highest.” [1]

Bhakti-Yoga is a real, genuine search after the Lord, beginning, continuing, and ending in love, with intense love to God being its essence.
“Bhakti-Yoga is a real, genuine search after the Lord, a search beginning, continuing, and ending in love. One single moment of the madness of extreme love to God brings us eternal freedom. "Bhakti", says Nârada in his explanation of the Bhakti-aphorisms, "is intense love to God"; "When a man gets it, he loves all, hates none; he becomes satisfied for ever"; "This love cannot be reduced to any earthly benefit", because so long as worldly desires last, that kind of love does not come; "Bhakti is greater than karma, greater than Yoga, because these are intended for an object in view, while Bhakti is its own fruition, its own means and its own end."” [2]

I say more on this in [Vol 3, Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion, Ch. 3: The Naturalness of Bhakti-Yoga and Its Central Secret]; [Vol 3, Bhakti-Yoga, Ch. 3: Spiritual Realisation, the Aim of Bhakti-Yoga].

question: What is Jnana-Yoga?

result.text:
Jnana-Yoga is the path of knowledge, aimed at realising our true divine nature.
“The word Jnâna means knowledge. It is derived from the root Jnâ — to know — the same word from which your English word to know is derived. Jnana-Yoga is Yoga by means of knowledge.” [1]

The object of Jnâna-Yoga is the same as that of Bhakti and Râja Yogas, but the method is different.
“The object of Jnâna-Yoga is the same as that of Bhakti and Râja Yogas, but the method is different. This is the Yoga for the strong, for those who are neither mystical nor devotional, but rational.” [2]

I say more on this in [Vol 5, Notes from Lectures and Discourses, On Jnana-Yoga].

question: What is the secret of work?

result.text:
The secret of work lies in performing it without attachment to results, with the mind focused on the act itself rather than on the outcome, and with the understanding that work is a means to spiritual growth and liberation.
“If working like slaves results in selfishness and attachment, working as master of our own mind gives rise to the bliss of non-attachment. We often talk of right and justice, but we find that in the world right and justice are mere baby's talk. There are two things which guide the conduct of men: might and mercy. The exercise of might is invariably the exercise of selfishness. All men and women try to make the most of whatever power or advantage they have. Mercy is heaven itself; to be good, we have all to be merciful. Even justice and right should stand on mercy. All thought of obtaining return for the work we do hinders our spiritual progress; nay, in the end it brings misery. There is another way in which this idea of mercy and selfless charity can be put into practice; that is, by looking upon work as "worship" in case we believe in a Personal God. Here we give up all the fruits our work unto the Lord, and worshipping Him thus, we have no right to expect anything from man kind for the work we do. The Lord Himself works incessantly and is ever without attachment. Just as water cannot wet the lotus leaf, so work cannot bind the unselfish man by giving rise to attachment to results. The selfless and unattached man may live in the very heart of a crowded and sinful city; he will not be touched by sin.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 2, Work and Its Secret]; [Vol 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, Unselfish Work Is True Renunciation]; [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 1: Karma in Its Effect on Character].

question: What is duty?

result.text:
Duty is a concept that varies according to different nations, states in life, and historical periods, and it is defined by the actions that align with one's conscience and moral training.
“It is necessary in the study of Karma-Yoga to know what duty is. If I have to do something I must first know that it is my duty, and then I can do it. The idea of duty again is different in different nations. The Mohammedan says what is written in his book, the Koran, is his duty; the Hindu says what is in the Vedas is his duty; and the Christian says what is in the Bible is his duty. We find that there are varied ideas of duty, differing according to different states in life, different historical periods and different nations. The term "duty", like every other universal abstract term, is impossible clearly to define; we can only get an idea of it by knowing its practical operations and results. When certain things occur before us, we have all a natural or trained impulse to act in a certain manner towards them; when this impulse comes, the mind begins to think about the situation. Sometimes it thinks that it is good to act in a particular manner under the given conditions; at other times it thinks that it is wrong to act in the same manner even in the very same circumstances. The ordinary idea of duty everywhere is that every good man follows the dictates of his conscience. But what is it that makes an act a duty?” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 7: Freedom].

question: What is Maya?

result.text:
Maya is not a theory, but a simple statement of facts — what we are and what we see around us.
“It is a simple statement of facts — what we are and what we see around us.” [1]

Maya is not a theory; it is simply a statement of facts about the universe as it exists.
“The translation of the word is neither happy nor correct.” [2]

Maya is not illusion as it is popularly interpreted.
“Maya is not illusion as it is popularly interpreted. Maya is real, yet it is not real. It is real in that the Real is behind it and gives it its appearance of reality. That which is real in Maya is the Reality in and through Maya. Yet the Reality is never seen; and hence that which is seen is unreal, and its has no real independent existence of itself, but is dependent upon the Real for its existence.” [3]

This eternal play of light and darkness — indiscriminate, indistinguishable, inseparable — is always there.
“This is a statement of facts, and this is what is called Maya.” [4]

I say more on this in [Vol 8, Writings: Prose, Cyclic Rest and Change]; [Vol 2, Jnana-Yoga, Ch. 5: Maya and Freedom]; [Vol 5, Questions and Answers, Selections from the Math Diary].

question: What is Prana?

result.text:
Prana is the energy that permeates the universe, manifesting in all forms of motion and life.
“The word used is Prâna. Prana is not exactly breath. It is the name for the energy that is in the universe. Whatever you see in the universe, whatever moves or works, or has life, is a manifestation of this Prana. The sum-total of the energy displayed in the universe is called Prana.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Ch. 3: Prana]; [Vol 1, Lectures and Discourses, The Soul and God]; [Vol 2, Jnana-Yoga, Ch. 15: The Real and the Apparent Man]; [Vol 2, Practical Vedanta and Other Lectures, Cosmology].

question: How should I practise meditation?

result.text:
I explain that meditation should begin with focusing on a single object to develop concentration.
“Swamiji: First, the practice of meditation has to proceed with some one object before the mind. Once I used to concentrate my mind on some black point. Ultimately, during those days, I could not see the point any more, nor notice that the point was before me at all — the mind used to be no more — no wave of functioning would rise, as if it were all an ocean without any breath of air. In that state I used to experience glimpses of supersensuous truth. So I think, the practice of meditation even with some trifling external object leads to mental concentration. But it is true that the mind very easily attains calmness when one practices meditation with anything on which one's mind is most apt to settle down. This is the reason why we have in this country so much worship of the images of gods and goddesses. And what wonderful art developed from such worship! But no more of that now. The fact, however, is that the objects of meditation can never be the same in the case of all men. People have proclaimed and preached to others only those external objects to which they held on to become perfected in meditation. Oblivious of the fact, later on, that these objects are aids to the attainment of perfect mental calmness, men have extolled them beyond everything else. They have wholly concerned themselves with the means, getting comparatively unmindful of the end.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, On Jnana-Yoga]; [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Patanjali's Yoga Aphorisms].

question: What is Pratyahara?

result.text:
Pratyahara is the process of gathering the mind inward and freeing it from the influence of the senses.
“He who has succeeded in attaching or detaching his mind to or from the centres at will has succeeded in Pratyahara, which means, "gathering towards," checking the outgoing powers of the mind, freeing it from the thraldom of the senses. When we can do this, we shall really possess character; then alone we shall have taken a long step towards freedom; before that we are mere machines.” [1]

Pratyahara involves checking the outgoing powers of the mind and focusing it on the desired object.
“Pratyahara is a gathering toward, an attempt to get hold of the mind and focus it on the desired object.” [2]

Pratyahara is the stage where the mind is no longer controlled by external objects but is brought under the will's control.
“When these come together and attach themselves to some external object, then we perceive it. At the same time it is a very difficult thing to concentrate the mind and attach it to one organ only; the mind is a slave.” [3]

Pratyahara is the act of bringing the senses under the control of the will, directing them inward rather than outward.
“Bringing them under the control of the will is what is called Pratyahara or gathering towards oneself.” [4]

I say more on this in [Vol 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, On Raja-Yoga]; [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Patanjali's Yoga Aphorisms]; [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Ch. 2: The First Steps].

question: What is Samadhi?

result.text:
Samadhi is a universal state that every being, from animals to angels, must reach for real religion to begin.
“Samadhi is the property of every human being — nay, every animal. From the lowest animal to the highest angel, some time or other, each one will have to come to that state, and then, and then alone, will real religion begin for him. Until then we only struggle towards that stage. There is no difference now between us and those who have no religion, because we have no experience. What is concentration good for, save to bring us to this experience? Each one of the steps to attain Samadhi has been reasoned out, properly adjusted, scientifically organised, and, when faithfully practiced, will surely lead us to the desired end. Then will all sorrows cease, all miseries vanish; the seeds for actions will be burnt, and the soul will be free for ever.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 7, Inspired Talks, Friday, July 5, 1895]; [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Patanjali's Yoga Aphorisms]; [Vol 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, On Raja-Yoga]; [Vol 4, Translation: Poems, The Hymn of Samadhi].

question: What is the Atman?

result.text:
The Atman is eternal and unchanging, never coming nor going, and is the true self beyond the illusions of the material world.
“The Atman never comes nor goes, is never born nor dies. It is nature moving before the Atman, and the reflection of this motion is on the Atman; and the Atman ignorantly thinks it is moving, and not nature. When the Atman thinks that, it is in bondage; but when it comes to find it never moves, that it is omnipresent, then freedom comes.” [1]

question: What is the real nature of man?

result.text:
The real nature of man is the Infinite, and he is struggling towards individuality, which is the same as the Infinite.
“We are struggling towards individuality, and that is the Infinite, that is the real nature of man. He alone lives whose life is in the whole universe, and the more we concentrate our lives on limited things, the faster we go towards death. Those moments alone we live when our lives are in the universe, in others; and living this little life is death, simply death, and that is why the fear of death comes. The fear of death can only be conquered when man realises that so long as there is one life in this universe, he is living. When he can say, "I am in everything, in everybody, I am in all lives, I am the universe," then alone comes the state of fearlessness. To talk of immortality in constantly changing things is absurd. Says an old Sanskrit philosopher: It is only the Spirit that is the individual, because it is infinite. No infinity can be divided; infinity cannot be broken into pieces. It is the same one, undivided unit for ever, and this is the individual man, the Real Man.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 8, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, I Am That I Am]; [Vol 7, Conversations and Dialogues, Sharat Chandra Chakravarty]; [Vol 7, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, The Destiny of Man]; [Vol 2, Reports in American Newspapers, Divinity of Man]; [Vol 5, Notes from Lectures and Discourses, On the Vedanta Philosophy].

question: Is the soul immortal?

result.text:
The soul is eternal and uncreated, as it is not composed of parts that can be disintegrated.
“Without birth or death, eternal, ever-existing is this soul of man.” [1]

Souls are eternal, not created, and cannot die.
“They also are eternal. No soul was [ever] created; neither can [the] soul die.” [2]

Because the soul is not made of matter, it is not subject to decomposition, and therefore must be immortal.
“This soul of man, because it is separate from the mind and body, because it is not composed of Akasha and Prana, must be immortal.” [3]

The soul must be eternal because it is not composed of any materials.
“The soul must also be eternal.” [4]

All religions, except primitive Buddhism, believe that man is a soul, an identity, a unit that never dies but is immortal.
“All religions, except primitive Buddhism, believe that man is a soul, an identity, a unit that never dies but is immortal.” [5]

I say more on this in [Vol 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, Notes on Vedanta]; [Vol 4, Writings: Prose, Reincarnation]; [Vol 1, Addresses at the Parliament of Religions, Paper on Hinduism]; [Vol 2, Practical Vedanta and Other Lectures, The Way to Blessedness].

question: What is the ideal of a universal religion?

result.text:
I believe that the ideal of a universal religion is not about forcing one single philosophy, mythology, or ritual upon all people, but about recognizing the diversity of expressions of truth and allowing each to find their own way to God.
“What then do I mean by the ideal of a universal religion? I do not mean any one universal philosophy, or any one universal mythology, or any one universal ritual held alike by all; for I know that this world must go on working, wheel within wheel, this intricate mass of machinery, most complex, most wonderful. What can we do then? We can make it run smoothly, we can lessen the friction, we can grease the wheels, as it were. How? By recognising the natural necessity of variation. Just as we have recognised unity by our very nature, so we must also recognise variation. We must learn that truth may be expressed in a hundred thousand ways, and that each of these ways is true as far as it goes. We must learn that the same thing can be viewed from a hundred different standpoints, and vet be the same thing. Take for instance the sun. Suppose a man standing on the earth looks at the sun when it rises in the morning; he sees a big ball. Suppose he starts on a journey towards the sun and takes a camera with him, taking photographs at every stage of his journey, until he reaches the sun.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 2, Practical Vedanta and Other Lectures, The Way to the Realisation of a Universal Religion].

question: What is the difference between religion and the religions?

result.text:
Religion, as I see it, is not confined to any one set of beliefs or practices, but is a universal force that expresses itself in many ways.
“The second idea that I learnt from my Master, and which is perhaps the most vital, is the wonderful truth that the religions of the world are not contradictory or antagonistic. They are but various phases of one eternal religion. That one eternal religion is applied to different planes of existence, is applied to the opinions of various minds and various races. There never was my religion or yours, my national religion or your national religion; there never existed many religions, there is only the one. One infinite religion existed all through eternity and will ever exist, and this religion is expressing itself in various countries in various ways. Therefore we must respect all religions and we must try to accept them all as far as we can. Religions manifest themselves not only according to race and geographical position, but according to individual powers. In one man religion is manifesting itself as intense activity, as work. In another it is manifesting itself as intense devotion, in yet another, as mysticism, in others as philosophy, and so forth. It is wrong when we say to others, "Your methods are not right." Perhaps a man, whose nature is that of love, thinks that the man who does good to others is not on the right road to religion, because it is not his own way, and is therefore wrong. If the philosopher thinks, "Oh, the poor ignorant people, what do they know about a God of Love, and loving Him?” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 6, Lectures and Discourses, The Vedanta Philosophy and Christianity]; [Vol 6, Lectures and Discourses, The Methods and Purpose of Religion]; [Vol 3, Lectures and Discourses, Unity, the Goal of Religion]; [Vol 1, Lectures and Discourses, Reason and Religion]; [Vol 2, Jnana-Yoga, Ch. 1: The Necessity of Religion]; [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Ch. 1: Introductory].

question: What is renunciation?

result.text:
Renunciation, according to me, is the total absence of all selfish motives, not merely abstinence from external contact.
“In the case of the Sannyasin, the end is the liberation of the Self and doing good to humanity — " "; and of the ways to attain it, the renunciation of Kama-Kanchana is the most important. Remember, renunciation consists in the total absence of all selfish motives and not in mere abstinence from external contact, such as avoiding to touch one's money kept with another at the same time enjoying all its benefits. Would that be renunciation?” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 8, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, Jnana and Karma]; [Vol 9, Conversations and Interviews, Renunciation].
