question: What is the meaning of 'each is great in his own place'?

result.text:
I explained that each person has their own unique role and greatness depending on their circumstances and duties.
“Then the Sannyasin said to the king, "King, you have seen that each is great in his own place. If you want to live in the world, live like those birds, ready at any moment to sacrifice yourself for others. If you want to renounce the world, be like that young man to whom the most beautiful woman and a kingdom were as nothing. If you want to be a householder, hold your life a sacrifice for the welfare of others; and if you choose the life of renunciation, do not even look at beauty and money and power. Each is great in his own place, but the duty of the one is not the duty of the other.” [1]

I emphasized that those who live in the world and those who renounce it are both great in their own ways.
“If a man retires from the world to worship God, he must not think that those who live in the world and work for the good of the world are not worshipping God: neither must those who live in the world, for wife and children, think that those who give up the world are low vagabonds. Each is great in his own place.” [2]

question: What is Para-Bhakti?

result.text:
Para-Bhakti is described as the highest form of devotion, characterized by an unbroken and steady focus of the mind and heart on the Lord with inseparable attachment.
“The higher knowledge is thus clearly shown to be the knowledge of the Brahman; and the Devi-Bhâgavata gives us the following definition of the higher love (Para-Bhakti): "As oil poured from one vessel to another falls in an unbroken line, so, when the mind in an unbroken stream thinks of the Lord, we have what is called Para-Bhakti or supreme love." This kind of undisturbed and ever-steady direction of the mind and the heart to the Lord with an inseparable attachment is indeed the highest manifestation of man's love to God. All other forms of Bhakti are only preparatory to the attainment of this highest form thereof, viz the Para-Bhakti which is also known as the love that comes after attachment (Râgânugâ).” [1]

question: What is the Ishta?

result.text:
The Ishta is derived from the root 'Ish,' meaning to desire or choose, and refers to the ideal or object of love and devotion that each individual must select according to their nature.
“The word Ishta is derived from the root Ish, to desire, choose.” [1]

The Ishta is the personality upon whom the disciple must concentrate for prayer and praise.
“The disciple must concentrate on a personality for prayer and praise, and that is his Ishta.” [2]

Each of us must have a sect, and that sect is our own Ishta — our own chosen way.
“Each of us must have a sect, and that sect is our own Ishta — our own chosen way.” [3]

By Ishta is meant the object of love and devotion.
“By Ishta is meant the object of love and devotion. . . .” [4]

I say more on this in [Vol 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora, Vedantism]; [Vol 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, Lessons on Bhakti-Yoga].

question: What is the need of a Guru?

result.text:
The need of a Guru is to help awaken spiritual life and quicken the higher powers of the soul, as every being requires external help to attain perfection.
“Every soul is destined to be perfect, and every being, in the end, will attain the state of perfection. Whatever we are now is the result of our acts and thoughts in the past; and whatever we shall be in the future will be the result of what we think end do now. But this, the shaping of our own destinies, does not preclude our receiving help from outside; nay, in the vast majority of cases such help is absolutely necessary. When it comes, the higher powers and possibilities of the soul are quickened, spiritual life is awakened, growth is animated, and man becomes holy and perfect in the end.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 8, Lectures and Discourses, Discipleship]; [Vol 5, Notes from Lectures and Discourses, Who Is a Real Guru?]; [Vol 7, Inspired Talks, Thursday, August 1, 1895]; [Vol 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora, What Have I Learnt?]; [Vol 5, Questions and Answers, Guru, Avatara, Yoga, Japa, Seva].

question: What does the Vedanta say about God?

result.text:
The Vedanta teaches that God is not a personal being, but an impersonal principle, and that every individual is a manifestation of this divine principle.
“What is the God of Vedanta? He is principle, not person. You and I are all Personal Gods. The absolute God of the universe, the creator, preserver, and destroyer of the universe, is impersonal principle. You and I, the cat, rat, devil, and ghost, all these are Its persons — all are Personal Gods. You want to worship Personal Gods. It is the worship of your own self. If you take my advice, you will never enter any church. Come out and go and wash off. Wash yourself again and again until you are cleansed of all the superstitions that have clung to you through the ages. Or, perhaps, you do not like to do so, since you do not wash yourself so often in this country — frequent washing is an Indian custom, not a custom of your society.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Lectures and Discourses, The Vedanta Philosophy]; [Vol 5, Notes from Lectures and Discourses, On the Vedanta Philosophy]; [Vol 2, Jnana-Yoga, Ch. 7: God in Everything].

question: What is the cause of evil in the world?

result.text:
I believe that the cause of evil in the world lies in the actions of man himself.
“With all dualistic theories the first difficulty is, how is it possible that under the rule of a just and merciful God, the repository of an infinite number of good qualities, there can be so many evils in this world? This question arose in all dualistic religions, but the Hindus never invented a Satan as an answer to it. The Hindus with one accord laid the blame on man, and it was easy for them to do so. Why? Because, as I have just now told you, they did not believe that souls were created out of nothing We see in this life that we can shape and form our future every one of us, every day, is trying to shape the morrow; today we fix the fate of the morrow; tomorrow we shall fix the fate of the day after, and so on. It is quite logical that this reasoning can be pushed backward too. If by our own deeds we shape our destiny in the future why not apply the same rule to the past? If, in an infinite chain, a certain number of links are alternately repeated then, if one of these groups of links be explained, we can explain the whole chain. So, in this infinite length of time, if we can cut off one portion and explain that portion and understand it, then, if it be true that nature is uniform, the same explanation must apply to the whole chain of time.” [1]

question: What is freedom?

result.text:
Blessedness, eternal peace, arising from perfect freedom, is the highest concept of religion underlying all the ideas of God in Vedanta — absolutely free Existence, not bound by anything, no change, no nature, nothing that can produce a change in Him.
“Blessedness, eternal peace, arising from perfect freedom, is the highest concept of religion underlying all the ideas of God in Vedanta — absolutely free Existence, not bound by anything, no change, no nature, nothing that can produce a change in Him. This same freedom is in you and in me and is the only real freedom.” [1]

Bondage and liberty, light and shadow, good and evil must be there, but the very fact of the bondage shows also this freedom hidden there.
“Bondage and liberty, light and shadow, good and evil must be there, but the very fact of the bondage shows also this freedom hidden there. If one is a fact, the other is equally a fact.” [2]

The object of the Jnana-Yoga is freedom.
“Freedom. Freedom from what?” [3]

One curious fact present in the midst of all our joys and sorrows, difficulties and struggles, is that we are surely journeying towards freedom.
“One curious fact present in the midst of all our joys and sorrows, difficulties and struggles, is that we are surely journeying towards freedom. The question was practically this: "What is this universe?” [4]

In the living there is freedom, there is intelligence; in the dead all is bound and no freedom is possible, because there is no intelligence.
“In the living there is freedom, there is intelligence; in the dead all is bound and no freedom is possible, because there is no intelligence. This freedom that distinguishes us from mere machines is what we are all striving for. To be more free is the goal of all our efforts, for only in perfect freedom can there be perfection. This effort to attain freedom underlies all forms of worship, whether we know it or not.” [5]

I say more on this in [Vol 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, Freedom of the Self]; [Vol 5, Notes from Lectures and Discourses, Law and Freedom]; [Vol 7, Inspired Talks, Saturday, July 13, 1895]; [Vol 4, Writings: Prose, Is the Soul Immortal?].

question: What is the ideal of Karma-Yoga?

result.text:
The ideal of Karma-Yoga is to attain freedom through unselfishness and good works, without needing to believe in any doctrine or even God.
“Karma-Yoga, therefore, is a system of ethics and religion intended to attain freedom through unselfishness, and by good works. The Karma-Yogi need not believe in any doctrine whatever. He may not believe even in God, may not ask what his soul is, nor think of any metaphysical speculation. He has got his own special aim of realising selflessness; and he has to work it out himself. Every moment of his life must be realisation, because he has to solve by mere work, without the help of doctrine or theory, the very same problem to which the Jnâni applies his reason and inspiration and the Bhakta his love.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 2: Each Is Great in His Own Place]; [Vol 8, Writings: Prose, Four Paths of Yoga].

question: What is the Sankhya cosmology?

result.text:
The Sankhya cosmology explains the universe as arising from the interaction of nature (Prakriti) and the soul (Purusha), with nature being composed of three fundamental qualities — Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas — that evolve into the universe through cycles of creation and dissolution.
“The system of Yoga is built entirely on the philosophy of the Sânkhyas, as I told you before, and here again I shall remind you of the cosmology of the Sankhya philosophy. According to the Sankhyas, nature is both the material and the efficient cause of the universe. In nature there are three sorts of materials, the Sattva, the Rajas, and the Tamas. The Tamas material is all that is dark, all that is ignorant and heavy. The Rajas is activity. The Sattva is calmness, light. Nature, before creation, is called by them Avyakta, undefined, or indiscrete; that is, in which there is no distinction of form or name, a state in which these three materials are held in perfect balance. Then the balance is disturbed, the three materials begin to mingle in various fashions, and the result is the universe. In every man, also, these three materials exist. When the Sattva material prevails, knowledge comes; when Rajas, activity; and when Tamas, darkness, lassitude, idleness, and ignorance. According to the Sankhya theory, the highest manifestation of nature, consisting of the three materials, is what they call Mahat or intelligence, universal intelligence, of which each human intellect is a part. In the Sankhya psychology there is a sharp distinction between Manas, the mind function, and the function of the Buddhi, intellect. The mind function is simply to collect and carry impressions and present them to the Buddhi, the individual Mahat, which determines upon it.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 2, Practical Vedanta and Other Lectures, Cosmology]; [Vol 2, Practical Vedanta and Other Lectures, A Study of the Sankhya Philosophy]; [Vol 2, Practical Vedanta and Other Lectures, Sankhya and Vedanta].

question: What are the three Gunas?

result.text:
The three Gunas are Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas, which are the fundamental substances that make up the sensible universe.
“The Gunas are the three substances, Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas, whose gross state is the sensible universe. Past and future arise from the different modes of manifestation of these Gunas.” [1]

question: What is the relation of Buddhism to Hinduism?

result.text:
I see Buddhism as a fulfillment of Hinduism, much like Christianity fulfilled Judaism, and I revere the Buddha as a great teacher whose teachings were not meant to destroy but to complete the spiritual path of the Hindus.
“I am not a Buddhist, as you have heard, and yet I am. If China, or Japan, or Ceylon follow the teachings of the Great Master, India worships him as God incarnate on earth. You have just now heard that I am going to criticise Buddhism, but by that I wish you to understand only this. Far be it from me to criticise him whom I worship as God incarnate on earth. But our views about Buddha are that he was not understood properly by his disciples. The relation between Hinduism (by Hinduism, I mean the religion of the Vedas) and what is called Buddhism at the present day is nearly the same as between Judaism and Christianity. Jesus Christ was a Jew, and Shâkya Muni was a Hindu. The Jews rejected Jesus Christ, nay, crucified him, and the Hindus have accepted Shâkya Muni as God and worship him. But the real difference that we Hindus want to show between modern Buddhism and what we should understand as the teachings of Lord Buddha lies principally in this: Shâkya Muni came to preach nothing new. He also, like Jesus, came to fulfil and not to destroy. Only, in the case of Jesus, it was the old people, the Jews, who did not understand him, while in the case of Buddha, it was his own followers who did not realise the import of his teachings.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 8, Sayings and Utterances]; [Vol 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, Notes Taken Down in Madras, 1892-93]; [Vol 3, Buddhistic India].

question: What is Advaita?

result.text:
Advaita is a philosophical system that teaches the ultimate reality is Brahman, and that everything else is an illusion or manifestation of Brahman.
“The Upanishads, the Vyâsa-Sutras, and the Gita, therefore, have been taken up by every sect in India that wants to claim authority for orthodoxy, whether dualist, or Vishishtâdvaitist, or Advaitist; the authorities of each of these are the three Prasthanas. We find that a Shankaracharya, or a Râmânuja, or a Madhvâchârya, or a Vallabhâcharya, or a Chaitanya — any one who wanted to propound a new sect —had to take up these three systems and write only a new commentary on them. Therefore it would be wrong to confine the word Vedanta only to one system which has arisen out of the Upanishads.” [1]

Advaita teaches that the universe is a continuous motion, and that individuality is only realized when one sees oneself as the whole universe.
“The Advaitist position is not merely a weak one of criticism. The Advaitist criticises others when they come too near him, and just throws them away, that is all; but he propounds his own position. He is the only one that criticises, and does not stop with criticism and showing books.” [2]

According to the Advaita philosophy, the universe does not exist at all; it is all illusion, and all beings are but reflections of the one Infinite Existence.
“So the non-dualists say, "This universe does not exist at all; it is all illusion. The whole of this universe, these Devas, gods, angels, and all the other beings born and dying, all this infinite number of souls coming up and going down, are all dreams." There is no Jiva at all.” [3]

I say more on this in [Vol 5, Writings: Prose and Poems, The Advaita Ashrama, Himalayas]; [Vol 2, Jnana-Yoga, Ch. 6: The Absolute and Manifestation]; [Vol 1, Lectures and Discourses, The Vedanta Philosophy]; [Vol 5, Interviews, With the Swami Vivekananda at Madura]; [Vol 5, Epistles, To Alasinga, U. S. a, 1895-05-06].

question: What is Dharma?

result.text:
I explain Dharma as that which impels man to seek happiness in this world or the next, and is established on work.
“With us, the prominent idea is Mukti; with the Westerners, it is Dharma. What we desire is Mukti; what they want is Dharma. Here the word "Dharma" is used in the sense of the Mimâmsakas. What is Dharma? Dharma is that which makes man seek for happiness in this world or the next. Dharma is established on work, Dharma is impelling man day and night to run after and work for happiness.” [1]

question: What is the meaning of the Gita's 'work without attachment'?

result.text:
The Gita teaches that if we do not attach ourselves to the work we do, it will not have any binding effect on our soul.
“The solution reached in the Gita in regard to this bondage-producing nature of work is that, if we do not attach ourselves to the work we do, it will not have any binding effect on our soul. We shall try to understand what is meant by this “non-attachment to” to work.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 7: Freedom].

question: How does one control the mind?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but the principles I have laid out provide a clear path. To control the mind, one must first study it, observing its wanderings and learning to fix it on a single idea through the power of will [1]. This requires systematic practice, beginning with Yama—controlling the mind by avoiding externals—and proceeding through Niyama, Âsana, Prânâyâma, Pratyâhâra, Dhâranâ, Dhyâna, and finally Samâdhi [2]. The mind must be restrained into smaller and smaller limits, and the subconscious must be explored, classified, and controlled to gain mastery over the conscious [3]. Regular breathing and the governance of the body also play a vital role in bringing the mind under control [4]. The purer the mind, the easier it is to control, and this purity is achieved through morality, truthfulness, and chastity. The mind, when trained and purified, becomes a powerful searchlight capable of reaching infinite scope [2]. Constant practice and non-attachment are essential to this process.

question: What is Om?

result.text:
Om is described as the manifesting word of God, the basis of all sounds, and a universal symbol representing the religious aspirations of humanity.
“The commentator says the manifesting word of God is Om. Why does he emphasise this word? There are hundreds of words for God. One thought is connected with a thousand words; the idea "God" is connected with hundreds of words, and each one stands as a symbol for God. Very good. But there must be a generalization among all time words, some substratum, some common ground of all these symbols, and that which is the common symbol will be the best, and will really represent them all. In making a sound we use the larynx and the palate as a sounding board. Is there any material sound of which all other sounds must be manifestations, one which is the most natural sound? Om (Aum) is such a sound, the basis of all sounds. The first letter, A, is the root sound, the key, pronounced without touching any part of the tongue or palate; M represents the last sound in the series, being produced by the closed lips, and the U rolls from the very root to the end of the sounding board of the mouth. Thus, Om represents the whole phenomena of sound-producing. As such, it must be the natural symbol, the matrix of all the various sounds. It denotes the whole range and possibility of all the words that can be made.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 7: Freedom].

question: What is the Vedanta's teaching on the many and the One?

result.text:
The Vedanta teaches that there is but one life, one world, and one existence, with all differences being only in degree, not in kind.
“For you must always remember that the one central ideal of Vedanta is this oneness. There are no two in anything, no two lives, nor even two different kinds of life for the two worlds. You will find the Vedas speaking of heavens and things like that at first; but later on, when they come to the highest ideals of their philosophy, they brush away all these things. There is but one life, one world, one existence. Everything is that One, the difference is in degree and not in kind. The difference between our lives is not in kind. The Vedanta entirely denies such ideas as that animals are separate from men, and that they were made and created by God to be used for our food.” [1]

question: What is love of God?

result.text:
I was asked how to worship, and I said to worship God as dearer than all possessions, relatives, and children, and as Love itself.

I explained that God is the infinite Love, and that nothing else in the universe matters as long as He is infinite love.
“That is the only definition of God. Do not care if this . . . universe is destroyed. What do we care as long as He is infinite love?” [2]

question: What are the four Yogas?

result.text:
The four Yogas are Karma-Yoga, Bhakti-Yoga, Râja-Yoga, and Jnâna-Yoga.
“Both the goal and the methods employed for reaching it are called Yoga, a word derived from the same Sanskrit root as the English "yoke", meaning "to join", to join us to our reality, God. There are various such Yogas, or methods of union — but the chief ones are — Karma-Yoga, Bhakti-Yoga, Râja-Yoga, and Jnâna-Yoga.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Ch. 8: Raja-Yoga in Brief]; [Vol 2, Practical Vedanta and Other Lectures, The Ideal of a Universal Religion].

question: What is the place of ritual and symbols in religion?

result.text:
Ritual and symbols are essential parts of every religion, as they help make abstract spiritual ideas more concrete and understandable.
“In every religion there are three parts: philosophy, mythology, and ritual. Philosophy of course is the essence of every religion; mythology explains and illustrates it by means of the more or less legendary lives of great men, stories and fables of wonderful things, and so on; ritual gives to that philosophy a still more concrete form, so that every one may grasp it — ritual is in fact concretised philosophy. This ritual is Karma; it is necessary in every religion, because most of us cannot understand abstract spiritual things until we grow much spiritually.” [1]

The study and practice of rituals and symbols form a natural part of Karma-Yoga, as they help convey religious thought to the minds of followers.
“In the world's ritualistic symbols we have an expression of the religious thought of humanity. It is easy to say that there is no use of rituals and temples and all such paraphernalia; every baby says that in modern times. But it must be easy for all to see that those who worship inside a temple are in many respects different from those who will not worship there. Therefore the association of particular temples, rituals, and other concrete forms with particular religions has a tendency to bring into the minds of the followers of those religions the thoughts for which those concrete things stand as symbols; and it is not wise to ignore rituals and symbology altogether. The study and practice of these things form naturally a part of Karma-Yoga.” [2]

I say more on this in [Vol 2, Bhakti or Devotion]; [Vol 4, Addresses on Bhakti-Yoga, The Need of Symbols]; [Vol 6, Lectures and Discourses, Formal Worship].

question: What is the Hindu idea of creation and cycles?

result.text:
The Hindu idea of creation and cycles is that creation is not a beginning from nothing, but a continuous projection of the infinite, with cycles of manifestation and dissolution repeating throughout eternity.
“The first is the question of creation, that this nature, Prakriti, Mâyâ is infinite, without beginning. It is not that this world was created the other day, not that a God came and created the world and since that time has been sleeping; for that cannot be. The creative energy is still going on. God is eternally creating — is never at rest. Remember the passage in the Gita where Krishna says, "If I remain at rest for one moment, this universe will be destroyed." If that creative energy which is working all around us, day and night, stops for a second, the whole thing falls to the ground. There never was a time when that energy did not work throughout the universe, but there is the law of cycles, Pralaya. Our Sanskrit word for creation, properly translated, should be projection and not creation. For the word creation in the English language has unhappily got that fearful, that most crude idea of something coming out of nothing, creation out of nonentity, non-existence becoming existence, which, of course, I would not insult you by asking you to believe. Our word, therefore, is projection.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Lectures and Discourses, Steps of Hindu Philosophic Thought].

question: What is reincarnation and why believe it?

result.text:
Reincarnation is the evolution of nature and the manifestation of the God within.
“Reincarnation is the evolution of nature and the manifestation of the God within.” [1]

The doctrine of reincarnation assumes an infinite importance to our mind, for the fight between reincarnation and mere cellular transmission is, in reality, the fight between spiritualism and materialism.
“It is thus that the doctrine of reincarnation assumes an infinite importance to our mind, for the fight between reincarnation and mere cellular transmission is, in reality, the fight between spiritualism and materialism. If cellular transmission is the all-sufficient explanation, materialism is inevitable, and there is no necessity for the theory of a soul. If it is not a sufficient explanation, the theory of an individual soul bringing into this life the experiences of the past is as absolutely true. There is no escape from the alternative, reincarnation or materialism.” [2]

The doctrine of reincarnation of the soul, while comparatively new and little understood in this country, is well-known in the east, being the foundation of nearly all the religions of those people.
“The doctrine of reincarnation of the soul, while comparatively new and little understood in this country, is well-known in the east, being the foundation of nearly all the religions of those people. Those that do not use it as dogma, do not say anything against it.” [3]

If you are going to exist in eternity hereafter, it must be that you have existed through eternity in the past: it cannot be otherwise.
“If you are going to exist in eternity hereafter, it must be that you have existed through eternity in the past: it cannot be otherwise. I will try to answer a few objections that are generally brought against the theory.” [4]

Reincarnation depends on Karma.
“Reincarnation depends on Karma. If a man accumulates Karma akin to the beastly nature, he will be drawn thereto.” [5]

question: What is the Absolute and manifestation?

result.text:
The Absolute is the reality behind the world, which appears through the veil of Maya or appearance.
“This world is "the evolution of nature and the manifestation of God". It is our interpretation of Brahman or the Absolute, seen through the veil of Mâyâ or appearance. The world is not zero, it has a certain reality; it only appears because Brahman is.” [1]

All that is real in nature is Brahman, seen through the illusion of Maya.
“All that is real in nature is Brahman, only it appears to be this variety, or nature, through the superimposition of Maya. Maya being illusion cannot be said to be real, yet it is producing the phenomena.” [2]

I say more on this in [Vol 2, Jnana-Yoga, Ch. 6: The Absolute and Manifestation]; [Vol 7, Inspired Talks, Wednesday, June 18, 1895]; [Vol 5, Questions and Answers, Discussions at the Graduate Philosophical Society]; [Vol 2, Practical Vedanta and Other Lectures, Sankhya and Vedanta].

question: What is the unity in diversity?

result.text:
The idea of unity in diversity is central to understanding the nature of truth and religious harmony, as it teaches that different perspectives on the same truth are valid and necessary.
“To learn this central secret that the truth may be one and yet many at the same time, that we may have different visions of the same truth from different standpoints, is exactly what must be done. Then, instead of antagonism to anyone, we shall have infinite sympathy with all. Knowing that as long as there are different natures born in this world, the same religious truth will require different adaptations, we shall understand that we are bound to have forbearance with each other.” [1]

The universe is a tremendous case of unity in variety, with the whole universe being a single mass of mind that manifests in different forms, yet remains one in essence.
“The whole universe is a tremendous case of unity in variety. There is only one mass of mind. Different [states] of that mind have different names. [They are] different little whirlpools in this ocean of mind. We are universal and individual at the same time. Thus is the play going on.... In reality this unity is never broken. [Matter, mind, spirit are all one.]” [2]

I say more on this in [Vol 2, Jnana-Yoga, Ch. 9: Unity in Diversity]; [Vol 5, Notes from Lectures and Discourses, On Jnana-Yoga].

question: What is the real worship?

result.text:
Real worship, according to me, is not found in ceremony, but in pure and sincere love in the heart.
“It is in love that religion exists and not in ceremony, in the pure and sincere love in the heart. Unless a man is pure in body and mind, his coming into a temple and worshipping Shiva is useless. The prayers of those that are pure in mind and body will be answered by Shiva, and those that are impure and yet try to teach religion to others will fail in the end. External worship is only a symbol of internal worship; but internal worship and purity are the real things. Without them, external worship would be of no avail. Therefore you must all try to remember this.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 2, Practical Vedanta and Other Lectures, Practical Vedanta: Part 2].

question: What is the ideal of womanhood in India?

result.text:
The ideal woman in India is the mother, and this idea is deeply rooted in Hindu culture.
“Now, the ideal woman in India is the mother, the mother first, and the mother last. The word woman calls up to the mind of the Hindu, motherhood; and God is called Mother. As children, every day, when we are boys, we have to go early in the morning with a little cup of water and place it before the mother, and mother dips her toe into it and we drink it.” [1]

In India, the mother holds a central position in the home, unlike the wife in the West.
“To the ordinary man in India, the whole force of womanhood is concentrated in motherhood. In the Western home, the wife rules. In an Indian home, the mother rules.” [2]

I say more on this in [Vol 8, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, Women of the East].

question: What is the use of concentration?

result.text:
Concentration is the one and only method of acquiring knowledge, as it allows the mind to focus and thus gain understanding.
“We have but one method of acquiring knowledge. From the lowest man to the highest Yogi, all have to use the same method; and that method is what is called concentration. The chemist who works in his laboratory concentrates all the powers of his mind, brings them into one focus, and throws them on the elements; and the elements stand analysed, and thus his knowledge comes. The astronomer has also concentrated the powers of his mind and brought them into one focus; and he throws them on to objects through his telescope; and stars and systems roll forward and give up their secrets to him. So it is in every case — with the professor in his chair, the student with his book — with every man who is working to know. You are hearing me, and if my words interest you, your mind will become concentrated on them; and then suppose a clock strikes, you will not hear it, on account of this concentration; and the more you are able to concentrate your mind, the better you will understand me; and the more I concentrate my love and powers, the better I shall be able to give expression to what I want to convey to you. The more this power of concentration, the more knowledge is acquired, because this is the one and only method of acquiring knowledge.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, Concentration]; [Vol 4, Lectures and Discourses, Concentration]; [Vol 6, Lectures and Discourses, Concentration and Breathing]; [Vol 7, Inspired Talks, Wednesday, July 24, 1895].

question: What is the mind according to Raja-Yoga?

result.text:
The mind and body are not separate entities; the mind is the internal substance that shapes the external form of the body, much like an oyster creates its shell.
“This body is just the external crust of the mind. They are not two different things; they are just as the oyster and its shell. They are but two aspects of one thing; the internal substance of the oyster takes up matter from outside, and manufactures the shell. In the same way the internal fine forces which are called mind take up gross matter from outside, and from that manufacture this external shell, the body.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Ch. 7: Dhyana and Samadhi].

question: Why is man divine?

result.text:
The Vedanta teaches that man is divine because all that is strong, good, and powerful in human nature is the outcome of that divinity, and every human being stands for the divine.
“One principle it lays down — and that, the Vedanta claims, is to be found in every religion in the world — that man is divine, that all this which we see around us is the outcome of that consciousness of the divine. Everything that is strong, and good, and powerful in human nature is the outcome of that divinity, and though potential in many, there is no difference between man and man essentially, all being alike divine. There is, as it were, an infinite ocean behind, and you and I are so many waves, coming out of that infinite ocean; and each one of us is trying his best to manifest that infinite outside. So, potentially, each one of us has that infinite ocean of Existence, Knowledge, and Bliss as our birthright, our real nature; and the difference between us is caused by the greater or lesser power to manifest that divine. Therefore the Vedanta lays down that each man should be treated not as what he manifests, but as what he stands for. Each human being stands for the divine, and, therefore, every teacher should be helpful, not by condemning man, but by helping him to call forth the divinity that is within him.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 3, Para-Bhakti or Supreme Devotion, Ch. 9: Human Representations of the Divine Ideal of Love]; [Vol 8, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, Man the Maker of His Destiny]; [Vol 6, Lectures and Discourses, Divine Love]; [Vol 1, Lectures and Discourses, The Hindu Religion]; [Vol 8, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, The Divine Incarnation or Avatara].

question: What is the secret of success in work?

result.text:
I have learned that paying as much attention to the means of work as to its end is one of the greatest lessons of life, and that this principle is the secret of success.
“One of the greatest lessons I have learnt in my life is to pay as much attention to the means of work as to its end. He was a great man from whom I learnt it, and his own life was a practical demonstration of this great principle I have been always learning great lessons from that one principle, and it appears to me that all the secret of success is there; to pay as much attention to the means as to the end.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, Unselfish Work Is True Renunciation]; [Vol 4, Writings: Prose, To My Brave Boys].

question: How should I handle burnout at work?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I can offer guidance rooted in the principles of Karma-Yoga and the understanding of work as a path to liberation. Burnout arises from attachment, expectation, and identification with the results of work. To handle it, you must detach your mind from the outcome and perform your duties as a witness, not as the doer. Remember, it is the mind and body that work, not you [1]. Let go of the idea that you are the cause of success or failure; instead, act with the understanding that you are merely an instrument of a greater will. Cultivate calmness and equanimity, for the less passion and expectation you have, the better you work and the more peace you find within [2]. When you give without desire, take without attachment, and remain unshaken by external circumstances, you will find that work no longer exhausts you, but becomes a means of spiritual growth and inner freedom [3].

question: I feel anxious about my career; what should I do?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I have often spoken of the remedy for anxiety and fear. When the mind is too anxious for the future, the only remedy is to go down on your knees — to surrender to the higher will, to trust in the divine plan [1]. Let not fear dominate your thoughts, for fear is the beginning of misery and disease [2]. Steel your heart and set yourself to work, for work is the true antidote to anxiety [3]. The world is waiting for those who are brave, sincere, and unselfish, and it is through work that we find our true purpose. Do not be afraid of the future; instead, be bold and daring, and work with all your might [4]. Remember, great things are in store for those who are willing to sacrifice for the good of others and for the progress of humanity. Have faith in yourself and in the divine; the work will progress by leaps and bounds if you remain steadfast and devoted.

question: How do I stay focused when my phone keeps distracting me?

result.text:
I did not speak to this directly, but I can offer guidance based on the principles I have shared. The key to concentration lies in training the mind to remain fixed on one object [1]. When distractions such as your phone arise, they are like external forces pulling your attention away. To counter this, you must gradually train your mind to resist these distractions, just as one trains the body through discipline [2]. This requires a scientific approach—gradually strengthening your ability to focus, rather than relying on force or sudden change. 

Furthermore, I have said that the mind must be turned back upon itself, and this is essential in the study of religion and in all deep work [3]. You must make a conscious effort to place your mind where you want it, not allow it to be drawn by external stimuli. Let the mind become steady and firm, like a mountain, unmoved by the winds of distraction. This is the path to true concentration.

question: My parents want me to marry; I want to pursue my studies abroad. What should I do?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I have much to say on the matter of duty and the pursuit of knowledge. The world is full of duties, but true freedom lies in doing them without attachment [1]. If your heart is drawn to study and the path of learning, and if you feel that your duty lies there, then you must follow it. Do not let the expectations of others bind you, for they may not know the depths of your soul. Marriage is a great duty, but it is not the only path to fulfillment. If you are called to study abroad, and if that call is strong within you, then go with courage. Let your parents know that you love them, but that your heart is set on a different course. The world needs thinkers, scholars, and visionaries. Let your actions be guided by the light of wisdom and the fire of your own aspirations.

question: How do I deal with a boss who takes credit for my work?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I can offer guidance rooted in the principles I have shared. The key lies in working for the good of others without seeking recognition or credit [1]. If a boss takes credit for your work, it is a test of your unselfishness and patience. Remember, the true worker cares nothing for results, but for the work itself [2]. Let your actions speak louder than words, and let your sincerity and love for the cause guide you. If you are driven by a higher motive—service to others—then no amount of misrepresentation can dim the light of your effort. Be the servant while leading, and never allow jealousy or a desire for acknowledgment to cloud your heart [3]. In time, the fruits of your labor will be seen, not by the boss, but by those who truly matter—the people you serve.

question: Is it wrong to want to be rich?

result.text:
I do not say it is bad to try to be rich.
“I do not say it is bad to try to be rich. It is marvellous, wonderful. Why, what does it show? It shows that one can have the same amount of energy and struggle for freedom as one has for money. We know we have to give up money and all other things when we die, and yet, see the amount of energy we can put forth for them. But we, the same human beings, should we not put forth a thousandfold more strength and energy to acquire that which never fades, but which remains to us for ever? For this is the one great friend, our own good deeds, our own spiritual excellence, that follows us beyond the grave. Everything else is left behind here with the body.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Karma-Yoga, Ch. 2: Each Is Great in His Own Place].

question: How should I raise my children in a city far from India?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but my principles may guide you. First, instill in them the values of compassion, self-discipline, and service to others, for these are the cornerstones of true education [1]. Let them grow in an environment where spiritual ideals are not separated from daily life, but are woven into it, just as our ancestors taught [1]. Encourage them to learn from the world around them, but never forget the importance of a strong and healthy body [2]. The child must be fed well, rested, and given the space to grow naturally. Even in a foreign land, teach them the dignity of labor, the value of knowledge, and the power of inner strength. Let them hear stories of great souls, of the wisdom of India, and of the eternal truths that bind all humanity [3]. Education must be oral at first, spoken through the ears, for it is through listening that the heart is stirred [4]. And always remember, the future of the child lies in the hands of the parents—nurture them with love, patience, and the light of wisdom.

question: How do I forgive someone who betrayed me?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but forgiveness is not a passive surrender, nor is it a sign of weakness. It is a strength that comes from within, a force that can transform both the forgiver and the forgiven. If you can forgive when you have the power to bring legions of angels to an easy victory, then that is true forgiveness; otherwise, it is merely cowardice [1]. To forgive someone who has betrayed you is not to forget the pain or to condone the betrayal, but to rise above it, to see the soul in the person who wronged you, and to let go of the anger that binds you. Renunciation, as taught by all the great prophets, is the key to purity of spirit [2]. It is not about giving up your rights, but about giving up the desire for revenge and the burden of hatred. Let the soul be like a lotus-leaf, untouched by the water in which it floats [1]. In this way, you become a true warrior, not of the flesh, but of the spirit.

question: What should a software engineer do to serve society?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I can reason from my principles. A software engineer, like any worker, must serve society by using his knowledge to uplift and benefit others. Technical education is essential for the progress of a nation, and through it, one can contribute to the development of industries and the betterment of human life [1]. The work of service must be done without distinction of caste or colour, and with a spirit of selflessness and dedication [2]. A software engineer must apply his skills to solve real-world problems, to build tools that make life easier, to promote justice, and to foster unity. He must not be driven by personal gain, but by the desire to serve others and to uplift the world [3]. In this way, he becomes a true worker for the good of all, fulfilling his duty and contributing to the great work of humanity. Let him remember that the world is in need of light, and he is one of those who can bring it through his service and wisdom.

question: How do I stop procrastinating?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I can offer guidance based on the principles of discipline and control of the mind. Procrastination is a form of allowing the mind to wander and be enslaved by external distractions, which is precisely what Yama and Pratyahara seek to address [1]. To stop procrastinating, you must first restrain the mind from external influences and train it to focus inward. This requires constant practice, patience, and non-attachment to worldly matters. Just as in Prânâyâma, where the breath is controlled through disciplined effort, so too must the mind be disciplined through daily practice [2]. Let the mind run freely at first, as a monkey jumping about, but do not be disturbed by its thoughts; simply watch and wait [3]. Over time, with persistent effort, the mind will become calmer and more focused. Remember, restraint does not come in one day, but by long continued practice [4]. As you cultivate self-control and inner purity, you will find that procrastination loses its hold over you.

question: How should I treat people who are rude to me online?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I would say that in the face of rudeness, one must remain steadfast in self-control and kindness. question: Is it okay to leave my religion?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I can say that renunciation is the heart of all spiritual growth, and it is not about abandoning one's religion in a superficial sense, but about moving beyond the limitations of form and ritual that bind the soul [1]. If one's religion has become a mere shell, filled with superstition and externalities, then it is indeed a hindrance, and one must move beyond it, just as a tree outgrows its hedge [3]. The goal is not to leave religion, but to transcend its limitations and reach the infinite, where all forms vanish and only the divine remains [4].

question: How do I deal with the fear of death?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but the foundation of my teachings offers a path. Fear of death arises from the illusion of separation from the universe and from the belief that we are bound to the body and its limitations [1]. To deal with this fear, you must realize your true nature — that you are not the body, but the eternal, unchanging Self, the infinite spirit, deathless and birthless [2]. When this realization dawns, fear vanishes, for you understand that death is an illusion, and you are beyond the reach of time and mortality. As I said, Whenever death approaches me, all weakness vanishes... I simply busy myself making ready to die [3]. This fearless attitude comes not from ignorance, but from the deep understanding that you are one with the universe, and that in this oneness, there is no fear, no death, only eternal bliss and freedom [1].

question: How can I be brave when I feel weak?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I have much to say on the subject of weakness and bravery. When you feel weak, it is not the weakness itself that is the enemy, but the fear of it. Be conscious of your dignity, and remember that within you lies the strength of the Divine Mother, the strength that has inspired countless souls to rise above fear and cowardice [1]. Let your heart be filled with love and faith, for it is love that gives power and courage [2]. When weakness comes, do not yield to it; instead, stamp it down with the firmness of a warrior. Remember the words of Râmprasâd: "Whom do I fear in the world, whose sovereign is the Divine Mother!" [1]. Let this pride in your spiritual heritage awaken the heroism within you. Be brave, for bravery is not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it. Struggle, and never be afraid. The world may seem full of enemies, but in your heart, let there be a land of friends, a land of strength and light [3].

If your heart is truly set on the spiritual, then their mockery will only serve to deepen your resolve and sharpen your purpose. Remember, the greatest spiritual heroes were often mocked in their time, yet they did not waver. Let their example be your guide.

question: How should a doctor handle the suffering of patients she cannot save?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I would say that the doctor's duty is not only to heal but also to comfort and to care for the suffering, even when recovery is not possible. The physician must nurse the body and the mind with equal diligence, for suffering is not merely physical but also mental and spiritual. Just as one would tend a wound or a burn with compassion and patience, so too must the doctor tend the afflicted soul, offering solace and dignity in the face of inevitable sorrow [1]. It is not enough to merely treat symptoms; the healer must also help the patient find meaning and peace in their suffering, guiding them toward a state of inner harmony. Even when death is near, the doctor must continue to act with love, for in that act lies the truest form of healing [2].

question: How do I handle jealousy of my more successful sibling?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I have often emphasized the importance of overcoming jealousy, for it is a great obstacle to spiritual and personal growth [1]. Jealousy is the bane of our race, and it must be rooted out from the heart [2]. When one sees another succeed, let that success be a source of inspiration rather than envy. Let it awaken in you the desire to rise, to work, to excel, and to do great deeds [3]. Remember, the moment jealousy or egoistic ideas come, resign yourself to the Lord, and make over your body and mind to His work [4]. Cultivate faith in yourself, and let that faith be the foundation upon which you build your own success [5]. Be ready to lend a hand to every worker of good, and send a good thought for every being in the three worlds [6]. Let your brother's success be a blessing, not a curse, and you will find peace and strength in your own journey.

question: What is the purpose of exercise and fitness?

result.text:
I emphasize the importance of physical strength and exercise for both personal well-being and the benefit of others.
“Swamiji: Another thing. You must learn to make the physique very strong and teach the same to others. Don't you find me exercising every day with dumb-bells even now? Walk in the morning and evenings and do physical labour. Body and mind must run parallel. It won't do to depend on others in everything. When the necessity of strengthening the physique is brought home to people, they will exert themselves of their own accord. It is to make them feel this need that education is necessary at the present moment.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Lectures and Discourses, Mohammed]; [Vol 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, The Practice of Religion].

question: How should I deal with anger at injustice I see in the news?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I would say that the root of all anger lies in the mind, and it is there that it must be subdued [1]. When you see injustice, your first reaction may be anger, but you must not identify with it. Anger is a wave of the mind, and like all waves, it must be met with a higher wave — that of love, compassion, and understanding [2]. Let your heart be filled with the desire to uplift and help, not to retaliate or curse. Remember, attachment to the unreal brings misery [3]. The world is full of suffering, and the more you identify with it, the more you become entangled in its chains. Instead, focus your energy on action — on working for the betterment of society, on spreading knowledge, and on cultivating within yourself the strength to remain calm amidst chaos. Let your anger be transformed into a force for good, and you shall find peace.

question: How do I keep my faith while studying science at university?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I can offer guidance grounded in the principles I have shared. Science and religion are not enemies; they are two paths leading to the same truth, each with its own methods and goals [1]. The science of religion, like the science of chemistry, seeks to find unity in diversity. In the same way, as a student of science, you may find that your studies reveal a deeper unity in the universe, a harmony that aligns with spiritual truths [2]. The challenge lies in not letting the blind faith of some scientists or the dogma of some religions cloud your understanding. Remain open, analytical, and cautious, as true science and true religion ask us to do [3]. Keep your faith by seeking unity in your studies, and let your understanding of the universe deepen both your scientific and spiritual perspectives. Faith is not blind belief, but a trust in the ultimate unity that science and religion both seek to reveal.

question: Should I give money to beggars?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but my teachings emphasize the spirit of giving and the importance of mutual benefit in all actions. To give without thought of return is a noble act, yet it should not be done in a way that perpetuates dependence or degradation [1]. If you give to a beggar, do so with compassion and understanding, but also consider whether your giving may inadvertently encourage a life of begging. True charity is not merely giving alms but uplifting the spirit and dignity of the recipient. In my view, the ideal is to give in a way that empowers, not merely to relieve immediate suffering [2]. The law of nature is to give and take in harmony, not to be always a beggar or always a giver [1]. Therefore, if you choose to give, do so with wisdom, and if you choose not to, do so with kindness, recognizing that the greatest gift is often the opportunity to rise above need.

question: How do I teach my students to be fearless?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but the essence of fearlessness lies in the realization of one's true nature as the infinite spirit, deathless and birthless [1]. Teach your students to look within and understand that they are not separate from the divine; they are the same as the Lord, and this knowledge alone can dissolve fear. Encourage them to see the world not as a battlefield of struggle and competition, but as a playground where all souls are playmates of the Divine [2]. Education is the key to this transformation [3]. Kindle their minds with the light of knowledge, and let them understand that they are not bound by their circumstances, but are the architects of their own destiny. Teach them that through realization, not mere words or rituals, they can become fearless. As I have said, "Be fearless, be fearless" [4]. When the student realizes that they are the same as the infinite, hope and strength will come naturally, and fear will vanish.

question: How do I remain humble after success?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I have much to say on the subject of humility and success. Humility is not the absence of pride, but the presence of true self-realization and the understanding that all achievements are but the result of past actions and the grace of the Divine. Remember, every successful man must have behind him tremendous integrity and sincerity, and this is the cause of his success [1]. True humility is the recognition that one is but a vessel through which the Divine works. The Bhakti-Yogi must hold himself as a dead man, never taking an insult, never retaliating [2]. Let success not make you arrogant, but rather deepen your reverence for the Guru and the Divine. Keep the pride of your spiritual lineage awake, and never allow weakness to overtake your mind [3]. Stay grounded in the realization that you are but a knower of Brahman, and that all glory belongs to the Divine.

question: What should I do about climate change?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I can offer some guidance based on my principles. Climate change is a modern challenge, and while it was not a question of my day, the spirit of my teachings may still apply. question: How can a working mother find time for spiritual practice?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I have much to say on the matter of balancing work and spiritual practice. A working mother, like all others, must find time for spiritual practice by making it a priority, even in the midst of daily duties. As I have said, meditation is the greatest thing, the nearest approach to spiritual life [1]. It is the moment when the mind is free from material concerns and turns inward. Even a quarter of an hour a day, if done with steadfast devotion, can bring great benefit [2]. Just as a mother fasts and prays for her child with unwavering love and sacrifice [3], so too must she find time for her own spiritual growth, for it is through her own inner peace that she can best serve her family. Let her remember that spiritual practice is not a luxury, but a necessity — a way to bring harmony to her life and to her work. It is through such devotion that the Divine Mother within will awaken and guide her [4].

question: How do I recover from a breakup?

result.text:
I did not speak to this directly, but I can offer guidance rooted in the principles I have shared. Recovery from a breakup is a matter of the heart and mind, and like all forms of sorrow, it must be transmuted into something greater. Do not dwell in silence upon your sorrows, for they will only grow heavier [1]. Instead, find ways to express your emotions—through art, work, or service to others. Let your heart be open, and allow the pain to flow through you, not stagnate within.

In my own struggles with illness and suffering, I found strength in movement, in cold water, and in the morning's vigorous exercise [2]. Similarly, in times of emotional pain, seek activity, seek light, and remember that even in your deepest sorrows, there is a soul of light [3]. Let this light guide you forward.

question: How do I handle criticism of my art?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but my teachings on criticism and art may guide you. I have always said that criticism, when excessive, is harmful and does not contribute to the progress of any work [1]. If you can with your whole heart produce one real thing, if you can rightly express a single idea in art, it must win appreciation in course of time [2]. A real thing never suffers from want of appreciation in this world. Do not be disheartened by criticism; instead, focus on the expression of truth and beauty. Criticizing others is not the way to reform; rather, you must criticise yourself and seek to understand the darkness within you [3]. If you are sincere in your work, the world will recognize it. Let your art be in touch with nature, yet strive to elevate it above nature, as true Art must be [4]. Let your heart be your guide, and your work shall speak for itself.

question: Is competition good for children?

result.text:
I did not speak to this directly, but I have much to say on the nature of competition and its effects on the young. Competition, as I have observed, is a force that often stands in the way of true progress and harmony [1]. It is not the cause of evolution, nor is it necessary for the development of the soul [1]. In fact, the more I have studied history, the more I have seen that war and competition have thrown back human progress rather than advanced it [1].  

Children, in their innocence, are born optimists, but the world they enter is one of constant disillusionment [2]. To subject them to the harshness of competition at an early age is to deny them the natural, healthy development they require. A strong and healthy body is the first step to virtue, and this must be nurtured with care [3]. Let us not push our children beyond their capacity, but rather teach them to grow in harmony with nature and with themselves.

question: How do I speak to my dying grandmother?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I can offer guidance rooted in the spiritual principles I have always emphasized. When addressing a dying loved one, speak with love, compassion, and sincerity. Let your words be a reflection of your innermost feelings, for it is in the heart that true communication resides. Remember that death is not an end, but a transition, and that the soul is eternal [1]. Do not fear the moment of parting; instead, see it as an opportunity to offer comfort, to express gratitude, and to remind your grandmother of the love that has bound you throughout your lives. In this sacred hour, let your voice be a vessel of peace, and your presence a source of light. As I have often said, the touch of the soul can transform even the darkest moments into ones of divine grace [2].

question: How do I stop comparing myself to others on social media?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I can offer guidance rooted in my teachings. Comparison is a form of illusion, a distraction from the true work of the soul. When you look to others on social media, you are seeing only fragments of their lives, not the whole. Each person is unique in their journey, and to measure yourself by another is to forget your own path [1]. Let your own ideal be your guide, and do the best you can to realise it. The more you focus on your own growth, the less power comparison will have over you. The world is not a stage for showing off, but a field for service and self-realisation. Stay rooted in your own purpose, and let others be as they are.

question: How do I deal with a corrupt official?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but my teachings offer guidance. Corruption is a disease that weakens the body of society, yet it is not the end of the road. We must not curse or condemn, but work with love and sympathy to restore what is broken [1]. If an official is corrupt, let us not abandon the institution, but seek to reform it from within. Let us not tear down the old edifice of our society, but clean and repair it, rather than replace it with something untested and possibly worse [2]. If you find yourself in a position where you must interact with such an official, do so with dignity and firmness, but never lose your own integrity. Remember, the light of truth and righteousness will always triumph over darkness [3]. Let your actions be guided by the principles of the Vedanta — carry the light of wisdom, and let it shine through your deeds. Work for the good of all, and trust that the Spirit will prevail in the long run.

question: How much should I sleep?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I have often observed the importance of rest and sleep in maintaining health and spiritual progress. In my own experience, I found that lying in bed and taking ample rest brought me much-needed sleep and improved digestion [1]. I have also noted that sleep is not the same as true rest, which comes through deep breathing and meditation, where the body and mind become rhythmical and harmonious [2]. Therefore, I would say that one should listen to the body and allow it the rest it needs, but also seek deeper rest through spiritual practices.

question: How do I keep calm during exams?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but my teachings on concentration and mental discipline may guide you. To keep calm during exams, begin by practicing controlled breathing, as I have often emphasized in my discussions on Pranayama [1]. Let the breath flow in and out rhythmically, and if possible, join it with the repetition of a sacred word like "Om." This will harmonize your system and bring a deep sense of rest, which is far greater than ordinary sleep [1]. Remember, calmness is not the absence of thought, but the mastery over it. When you are calm and breathing equally through both nostrils, you are in the right condition for quiet meditation and clear thinking [3]. With constant practice and non-attachment, you can bring the same calmness into your exams.

question: Should I become a monk or stay a householder?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I have often emphasized that neither path is inherently superior to the other. The householder and the monk each have their own great duties, and both are equally sacred in the eyes of God [1]. The life of the householder is no less glorious than that of the monk, for it is far more difficult to live in the world and remain devoted to God, performing one's duties with sincerity and detachment [1]. The householder must be a hero to his enemies, gentle to his friends, and the foundation of society [2]. At the same time, the monk's life is one of complete dedication to spiritual pursuits, and he must be respected and honored by all [3]. The choice between these paths depends upon one's nature, circumstances, and the call of the Divine. If you are called to the life of a householder, then do so with courage and devotion. If the call is to renunciation, then follow it with equal earnestness. Both paths lead to the same goal, if pursued with sincerity.

question: How do I practise non-attachment while loving my family?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but the principles of non-attachment are clear in my teachings. Non-attachment does not mean to abandon love or duty, but to perform actions without being bound by the results or the sense of ownership [1]. When you love your family, you do so with the understanding that they are not yours to possess, but part of the divine plan. You act as a nurse who cares for a child, knowing that when the time comes, you will leave without sorrow [2]. Love them, serve them, but do not allow your mind to be tied to their happiness or sorrow. Let your actions be offerings to the Lord, and your heart remain free [3]. This is the true way of non-attachment — to give without expectation, to love without clinging, and to remain at peace in all conditions [4].

question: How do I deal with guilt over past mistakes?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I have much to say on the matter. The past is a seed, and like all seeds, it holds within it the potential for growth, whether for good or for ill. The mistakes of the past are not to be moaned over, but used as guides for the future [1]. To dwell on guilt is to remain shackled by the chains of the past, when the true path lies in recognizing that you are the creator of your own destiny [2]. Say to yourself, This misery that I suffer is of my own doing, and from that admission rise with renewed strength. The past cannot be changed, but it can teach you. As I have said, Blessed be the mistakes, for they have been angels unawares [3]. Let them be lessons, not burdens. Take full responsibility, and know that within you lies the power to rise above all that has been. Let the dead past bury its dead, and march forward with the infinite future before you.

question: What should I do with my inheritance?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but the principles I have emphasized can guide you. Inheritance, like wealth, should not be seen as an end in itself, but as a means to higher ends. If you have received something from your ancestors, consider it a trust, a responsibility to use it for the upliftment of others and the cultivation of your own spiritual life [1]. The true heritage we inherit is not merely material, but also the potential for goodness, wisdom, and service [2]. Just as the householder is called to use his wealth nobly for the welfare of society, so too should you use your inheritance with a spirit of self-sacrifice and devotion [3]. Let it be a means to leave a heritage of good to your successors, and to help in the onward march of accumulated goodness for the world's sake [4].

question: How do I become a better listener?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I would say that becoming a better listener begins with cultivating the mind's power of attention. The mind, when properly guided, can be trained to focus and remain undistracted, whether in hearing, seeing, or tasting [1]. Just as concentration comes from various sources, such as hearing beautiful music or seeing beautiful scenery [2], so too can one train the mind to listen with deeper awareness. This requires practice, patience, and the ability to turn the mind inward, to observe its own workings, and to stop it from being carried away by external distractions [3]. To listen truly is to hear not just with the ears, but with the heart and the soul. Let your listening be like a bulldog's grip — firm, focused, and unwavering [4].

question: How do I serve the poor without becoming proud of it?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I can offer guidance rooted in my teachings. To serve the poor without pride, one must first understand that the act of helping is not about the giver, but about the humility and love that inspire it. When you give, do not see yourself as superior or noble, but as a vessel through which God’s grace flows [1]. Think of the poor not as objects of pity, but as equals, as manifestations of the divine, and as opportunities to practice true compassion without expectation of return [2]. The moment you begin to feel pride in your service, you have already lost the essence of it. Let your actions be silent, unattached, and free from the desire for recognition or reward. In this way, you do not become proud, for your heart remains humble and your work remains pure [3].

question: How can I stop being afraid of public speaking?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but my teachings on fear and courage may guide you. Fear is a natural part of the human condition, but it must not rule your life. Steel your heart and set yourself to work, for the mind is a battlefield where courage is forged [1]. When you stand before an audience, remember that it is not your ego that must speak, but the divine within you. If you have faith in the higher power, you will find strength in the moment [2]. Go on saying, "I am free," even when fear whispers otherwise [3]. Public speaking is a test of your will, and with each attempt, you will grow stronger. Do not fear failure, for it is through failure that we learn. The voice of the majority may be wrong, and every new thought must create opposition, but that is the price of truth [2]. Be bold, be fearless, and let the Lord be your strength.

question: How do I find my purpose in life?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I can guide you with what I have taught. The purpose of life is not something external to be found, but something within, to be realized. We are all seeking the same truth, though we express it in different ways [1]. This truth is the realization of the Self, the Atman, the one infinite being that is within and beyond all [2]. The longing for this blissful universe is in all hearts, and it is the goal of all religion [1]. To find your purpose, look inward. Realize that you are not the limited "I" that you think you are, but the infinite Self, the same in all beings. Let go of the small self, the ego, and seek the Eternal Unity. This is the path to true peace and fulfillment. It is not found in external achievements or possessions, but in the realization of your true nature [2].

question: Do you reject dualism in favour of Advaita?

result.text:
I do not reject dualism, for it is one of the necessary steps on the path to Advaita.
“Our solution is that the Advaita is not antagonistic to the Dvaita (dualism). We say the latter is only one of three steps. Religion always takes three steps. The first is dualism. Then man gets to a higher state, partial non-dualism. And at last he finds he is one with the universe. Therefore the three do not contradict but fulfil.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 2, Practical Vedanta and Other Lectures, Practical Vedanta: Part 4]; [Vol 1, Lectures and Discourses, The Vedanta Philosophy].

question: Is Advaita compatible with reason?

result.text:
I believe that Advaita is compatible with reason, as it aligns with modern scientific research and satisfies intellectual needs.
“I may make bold to say that the only religion which agrees with, and even goes a little further than modern researches, both on physical and moral lines is the Advaita, and that is why it appeals to modern scientists so much. They find that the old dualistic theories are not enough for them, do not satisfy their necessities.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Lectures and Discourses, Reason and Religion].

question: Is caste part of religion?

result.text:
The caste system is opposed to the religion of the Vedanta, as it is a social custom, not a religious one.
“The caste system is opposed to the religion of the Vedanta. Caste is a social custom, and all our great preachers have tried to break it down. From Buddhism downwards, every sect has preached against caste, and every time it has only riveted the chains.” [1]

The caste system has nothing to do with religion, as a man's occupation is hereditary.
“"The caste system has nothing to do with religion. A man's occupation is hereditary — a carpenter is born a carpenter: a goldsmith, a goldsmith; a workman, a workman: and a priest, a priest.” [2]

In religion there is no caste; caste is simply a social institution.
“In religion there is no caste; caste is simply a social institution.” [3]

Caste is a social organization and not a religious one.
“Caste is a social organization and not a religious one. It was the outcome of the natural evolution of our society.” [4]

Similar is the case with the caste system and other social customs.
“Similar is the case with the caste system and other social customs.” [5]

I say more on this in [Vol 5, Questions and Answers, Discussions at the Graduate Philosophical Society]; [Vol 6, Writings: Prose and Poems, Historical Evolution of India].

question: Should hereditary privilege continue?

result.text:
No, hereditary privilege should not continue, as it is a form of unjust advantage that Vedanta explicitly rejects.
“None can be Vedantists, and at the same time admit of privilege to anyone, either mental, physical, or spiritual; absolutely no privilege for anyone.” [1]

The work of the Advaita is to eliminate all forms of privilege, including those based on birth.
“But what can be attained is elimination of privilege.” [2]

Even though differences in wealth, strength, or knowledge exist, no one should have more privilege than another, as all are equal in their potential to express the divine message.
“Let us remain so, but because you are physically or intellectually stronger, you must not have more privilege than I, and that you have more wealth is no reason why you should be considered greater than I, for that sameness is here, in spite of the different conditions.” [3]

I say more on this in [Vol 4, Translation: Prose, Modern India]; [Vol 9, Lectures and Discourses, The First Step Towards Jnana].

question: How should the caste problem be solved?

result.text:
I believe the solution to the caste problem in India lies not in degrading the higher castes or crushing out the Brahmin, but in elevating all through the ideal of Brahminhood.
“The solution of the caste problem in India, therefore, assumes this form, not to degrade the higher castes, not to crush out the Brahmin. The Brahminhood is the ideal of humanity in India, as wonderfully put forward by Shankaracharya at the beginning of his commentary on the Gitâ, where he speaks about the reason for Krishna's coming as a preacher for the preservation of Brahminhood, of Brahminness. That was the great end. This Brahmin, the man of God, he who has known Brahman, the ideal man, the perfect man, must remain; he must not go. And with all the defects of the caste now, we know that we must all be ready to give to the Brahmins this credit, that from them have come more men with real Brahminness in them than from all the other castes. That is true. That is the credit due to them from all the other castes. We must be bold enough, must be brave enough to speak of their defects, but at the same time we must give the credit that is due to them. Remember the old English proverb, "Give every man his due". Therefore, my friends, it is no use fighting among the castes. What good will it do? It will divide us all the more, weaken us all the more, degrade us all the more.” [1]

question: What is the ideal of womanhood?

result.text:
In the West, the ideal of womanhood is concentrated in the role of the wife, whereas in India, it is centered on motherhood, where the mother is revered as the giver of life and the founder of the race.
“In the West, the woman is wife. The idea of womanhood is concentrated there — as the wife. To the ordinary man in India, the whole force of womanhood is concentrated in motherhood. In the Western home, the wife rules. In an Indian home, the mother rules. If a mother comes into a Western home, she has to be subordinate to the wife; to the wife belongs the home. A mother always lives in our homes: the wife must be subordinate to her. See all the difference of ideas.” [1]

In India, the ideal of womanhood is deeply tied to motherhood, with the mother being revered and seen as the giver of life and the founder of the race.
“The speaker closed with comparing the position of women in India with that of this country. In India the whole idea of womanhood is the mother. The mother is reverenced. She is the giver of life, the founder of the race.” [2]

I say more on this in [Vol 8, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, Women of the East].

question: Can a nation rise without honouring women?

result.text:
I have seen women in statesmanship and governance prove themselves equal, if not superior, to men.
“Women in statesmanship, managing territories, governing countries, even making war, have proved themselves equal to men — if not superior. In India I have no doubt of that. Whenever they have had the opportunity, they have proved that they have as much ability as men, with this advantage — that they seldom degenerate. They keep to the moral standard, which is innate in their nature. And thus as governors and rulers of their state, they prove — at least in India — far superior to men. John Stuart Mill mentions this fact.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 8, Lectures and Discourses, Women of India].
