question: How do Hinduism and Buddhism relate?

result.text:
I see Buddhism as a fulfillment of Hinduism, not a separate or opposing religion.
“I am not a Buddhist, as you have heard, and yet I am. If China, or Japan, or Ceylon follow the teachings of the Great Master, India worships him as God incarnate on earth. You have just now heard that I am going to criticise Buddhism, but by that I wish you to understand only this. Far be it from me to criticise him whom I worship as God incarnate on earth. But our views about Buddha are that he was not understood properly by his disciples. The relation between Hinduism (by Hinduism, I mean the religion of the Vedas) and what is called Buddhism at the present day is nearly the same as between Judaism and Christianity. Jesus Christ was a Jew, and Shâkya Muni was a Hindu. The Jews rejected Jesus Christ, nay, crucified him, and the Hindus have accepted Shâkya Muni as God and worship him. But the real difference that we Hindus want to show between modern Buddhism and what we should understand as the teachings of Lord Buddha lies principally in this: Shâkya Muni came to preach nothing new. He also, like Jesus, came to fulfil and not to destroy. Only, in the case of Jesus, it was the old people, the Jews, who did not understand him, while in the case of Buddha, it was his own followers who did not realise the import of his teachings.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 3, Buddhistic India]; [Vol 4, Translation: Prose, The Paris Congress of the History of Religions]; [Vol 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, Notes Taken Down in Madras, 1892-93].

question: What do you think of Buddha?

result.text: I have more veneration for the character of Buddha than for any other — his boldness, fearlessness, and tremendous love for humanity.[1] The life of Buddha has an especial appeal, and he was born for the good of men, seeking truth not for himself but for the relief of others in misery.[1] I have always been very fond of Buddha, though not of his doctrine, and I believe he was one of the greatest men of renunciation ever born.[2] Buddhism is historically the most important religion, as it was the most tremendous religious movement ever seen, with effects felt across all civilizations.[3] Buddha was against the caste system, priestcraft, and metaphysical discussions, and he preached a religion of selfless action and no motive power.[4] He did not concern himself with metaphysical theories about God, but instead focused on right conduct, saying, 'Do good and be good.'[4] I believe that the monastic vow was preached more thoroughly all over India since the time of Buddha, and renunciation became the highest aim of religious life.[2]

question: Why did Buddhism decline in India?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I have often reflected on the reasons behind Buddhism's decline in India. Buddhism, though a noble and profound philosophy, lacked the necessary strength to sustain itself in the socio-political structure of India. It did not address the practical needs of the people, nor did it possess the means to control or influence the ruling powers [1]. The Buddhist monks, being renouncers of the world, lived in monasteries, unconcerned with secular affairs, and thus could not bring the royal power under their control [1]. The introduction of foreign customs and the breakdown of traditional structures further weakened Buddhism, leading to a reaction that ultimately revived the ancient Hindu philosophies [2]. The revival was led by Shankara, who brought back the Vedas to life, and modern Hinduism thus became a blend of ancient and new ideas [2]. Buddhism, unable to adapt to the changing times, eventually faded from the land of its birth.

question: Are rituals necessary?

result.text:
Rituals are essential for the current state of the world, and new ones must be created to replace outdated ones.
“"Rituals are the kindergarten of religion. They are absolutely necessary for the world as it is now; only we shall have to give people newer and fresher rituals. A party of thinkers must undertake to do this.” [1]

It is absolutely necessary to form some ritual and have a Church, as a loose system of philosophy gets no hold on mankind.
“It is absolutely necessary to form some ritual and have a Church. That is to say, we must fix on some ritual as fast as we can.” [2]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Lectures and Discourses, Vedic Religious Ideals].

question: How should one worship God?

result.text:
I explain that worship involves seeing God as the ultimate love, more dear than anything else, and that all other thoughts must vanish except for Him.
“The question was asked: How to worship? Worship Him as dearer than all your possessions, dearer than all your relatives, [dearer than] your children. [Worship Him as] the one you love as Love itself. There is one whose name is infinite Love. That is the only definition of God. Do not care if this . . . universe is destroyed. What do we care as long as He is infinite love? [Do you see what worship means? All other thoughts must go. Everything must vanish except God. The love the father or mother has for the child, [the love] the wife [has] for the husband, the husband, for the wife, the friend for the friend — all these loves concentrated into one must be given to God. Now, if the woman loves the man, she cannot love another man. If the man loves the woman, he cannot love another [woman]. Such is the nature of love.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 6, Lectures and Discourses, Worshipper and Worshipped]; [Vol 4, Addresses on Bhakti-Yoga, The Teacher of Spirituality].

question: Should religion be preached to the starving?

result.text:
I criticize the focus on converting souls rather than addressing physical suffering, arguing that offering religion to the starving is an insult.
“Christians must always be ready for good criticism, and I hardly think that you will mind if I make a little criticism. You Christians, who are so fond of sending out missionaries to save the soul of the heathen — why do you not try to save their bodies from starvation? In India, during the terrible famines, thousands died from hunger, yet you Christians did nothing. You erect churches all through India, but the crying evil in the East is not religion — they have religion enough — but it is bread that the suffering millions of burning India cry out for with parched throats. They ask us for bread, but we give them stones. It is an insult to a starving people to offer them religion; it is an insult to a starving man to teach him metaphysics. In India a priest that preached for money would lose caste and be spat upon by the people. I came here to seek aid for my impoverished people, and I fully realised how difficult it was to get help for heathens from Christians in a Christian land.” [1]

question: Is renunciation necessary for religion?

result.text:
Religion, according to my teachings, is fundamentally rooted in renunciation.
“We have now finished the consideration of what may be called the preparatory Bhakti, and are entering on the study of the Parâ-Bhakti or supreme devotion. We have to speak of a preparation to the practice of this Para-Bhakti. All such preparations are intended only for the purification of the soul. The repetition of names, the rituals, the forms, and the symbols, all these various things are for the purification of the soul. The greatest purifier among all such things, a purifier without which no one can enter the regions of this higher devotion (Para-Bhakti), is renunciation. This frightens many; yet, without it, there cannot be any spiritual growth. In all our Yogas this renunciation is necessary. This is the stepping-stone and the real centre and the real heart of all spiritual culture — renunciation. This is religion — renunciation.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 4, Lectures and Discourses, Christ, the Messenger].

question: Must one renounce the world to be religious?

result.text:
Renunciation is essential for realizing the spirit as spirit, achieved through renouncing the senses and cutting the chains that bind us to matter.
“Therefore to realise the spirit as spirit is practical religion. Everything else is good so far as it leads to this one grand idea. That [realization] is to be attained by renunciation, by meditation — renunciation of all the senses, cutting the knots, the chains that bind us down to matter. "I do not want to get material life, do not want the sense-life, but something higher." That is renunciation. Then, by the power of meditation, undo the mischief that has been done.” [1]

Renunciation is not asceticism, but a mental state where one sees the world as unreal, like a mirage.
“But does renunciation demand that we all become ascetics? Who then is to help others? Renunciation is not asceticism. Are all beggars Christ? Poverty is not a synonym for holiness; often the reverse. Renunciation is of the mind. How does it come? In a desert, when I was thirsty, I saw a lake.” [2]

To be spiritual, one must renounce the world mentally, even if not physically, and have Vairâgya (renunciation).
“Give up, renounce the world. Now we are like dogs strayed into a kitchen and eating a piece of meat, looking round in fear lest at any moment some one may come and drive them out. Instead of that, be a king and know you own the world. This never comes until you give it up and it ceases to bind. Give up mentally, if you do not physically. Give up from the heart of your hearts. Have Vairâgya (renunciation). This is the real sacrifice, and without it, it is impossible to attain spirituality.” [3]

I say more on this in [Vol 8, Lectures and Discourses, Discipleship]; [Vol 5, Epistles, To S--, U. S. a, 1895-05-02].

question: Should religion submit to reason?

result.text:
I believe that religion must be judged by the standard of reason, as it is the only way to determine truth in any matter.
“Now, the question arises if this light of reason is able to judge between inspiration and inspiration, and if this light can uphold its standard when the quarrel is between prophet and prophet, if it has the power of understanding anything whatsoever of religion. If it has not, nothing can determine the hopeless fight of books and prophets which has been going on through ages; for it means that all religions are mere lies, hopelessly contradictory, without any constant idea of ethics. The proof of religion depends on the truth of the constitution of man, and not on any books.” [1]

Reason is the universal standard by which all things, including religion, must be judged, for it is the only way to resolve contradictions and determine what is truly ethical.
“Everything it claims must be judged from the standpoint of reason. Why religions should claim that they are not bound to abide by the standpoint of reason, no one knows. If one does not take the standard of reason, there cannot be any true judgment, even in the case of religions.” [2]

question: Does science contradict Vedanta?

result.text:
Modern science and Vedanta are in harmony, as the conclusions of science align with those of Vedanta, according to my experience and observations.
“It seems clear that the conclusions of modern materialistic science can be acceptable, harmoniously with their religion, only to the Vedantins or Hindus as they are called. It seems clear that modern materialism can hold its own and at the same time approach spirituality by taking up the conclusions of the Vedanta. It seems to us, and to all who care to know, that the conclusions of modern science are the very conclusions the Vedanta reached ages ago; only, in modern science they are written in the language of matter. This then is another claim of the Vedanta upon modern Western minds, its rationality, the wonderful rationalism of the Vedanta. I have myself been told by some of the best Western scientific minds of the day, how wonderfully rational the conclusions of the Vedanta are. I know one of them personally who scarcely has time to eat his meal or go out of his laboratory, but who yet would stand by the hour to attend my lectures on the Vedanta; for, as he expresses it, they are so scientific, they so exactly harmonise with the aspirations of the age and with the conclusions to which modern science is coming at the present time.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora, The Vedanta]; [Vol 8, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, The Claims of Vedanta on the Modern World]; [Vol 3, Lectures and Discourses, Unity, the Goal of Religion]; [Vol 2, Practical Vedanta and Other Lectures, Cosmology].

question: Are other religions true?

result.text:
I have studied many religions and found that they all lead to the same truth, though expressed in different ways.
“"The next question that arises," said he, "are these religions true or are some of them true and some of them false? They have all reached one conclusion, that of an absolute and infinite existence. Unity is the object of religion. The multiple of phenomena that is seen at every hand is only the infinite variety of unity. An analysis of religion shows that man does not travel from fallacy to truth, but from a lower truth to a higher truth.” [1]

Religion is not about error, but about progressing from one truth to a higher truth.
“In all religions we travel from a lesser to a higher truth, never from error to truth. There is a Oneness behind all creation, but minds are very various. 'That which exists is One, sages call It variously.' What I mean is that one progresses from a smaller to a greater truth. The worst religions are only bad readings of the froth. One gets to understand bit by bit. Even devil-worship is but a perverted reading of the ever-true and immutable Brahman. Other phases have more or less of the truth in them. No form of religion possesses it entirely.” [2]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Lectures and Discourses, Soul, God and Religion]; [Vol 2, Practical Vedanta and Other Lectures, The Way to the Realisation of a Universal Religion]; [Vol 4, Lectures and Discourses, My Master]; [Vol 6, Lectures and Discourses, The Vedanta Philosophy and Christianity]; [Vol 1, Lectures and Discourses, Reason and Religion].

question: Should Hindus convert others?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I have made it clear that Hinduism is not a religion that seeks to convert others [1]. It is all-receptive, all-embracing, and all-comprehensive, caring not to oppose the progress of Christianity or any other religion. Its strength lies in its infinite adaptability to the infinite diversity of human characters and tendencies. Therefore, it is not the duty of Hindus to convert others, but rather to live by their principles and let their example speak. If others are drawn to Hinduism, it is by their own will and understanding, not by force or persuasion. I have also stated that India can never be converted to Christianity, and that the conditions of the lower classes are not made better by Christianity [2]. My message is one of harmony, not conversion.

Education is not merely about knowledge, but about the training of will and character.

To me, the very essence of education is concentration of mind, not the collecting of facts.
“To me the very essence of education is concentration of mind, not the collecting of facts.” [3]

Education is not the amount of information that is put into your brain and runs riot there, undigested, all your life.

question: What is the aim of education?

result.text:
Education, to me, is not merely about book-learning or the accumulation of knowledge, but about the formation of character, the expansion of the intellect, and the development of strength of mind.
“Swamiji: Certainly. But education should be imparted along with it, otherwise irregularity and corruption will ensue. By education I do not mean the present system, but something in the line of positive teaching. Mere book-learning won't do. We want that education by which character is formed, strength of mind is increased, the intellect is expanded, and by which one can stand on one's own feet.” [1]

The ideal of education, I believe, is to make a man, to develop the inner self, and to create a personality that can influence others and achieve great things.
“The ideal of all education, all training, should be this man-making. But, instead of that, we are always trying to polish up the outside. What use in polishing up the outside when there is no inside? The end and aim of all training is to make the man grow. The man who influences, who throws his magic, as it were, upon his fellow-beings, is a dynamo of power, and when that man is ready, he can do anything and everything he likes; that personality put upon anything will make it work.” [2]

To me, the essence of education is the development of concentration and detachment, which allows one to collect facts at will and use them effectively.
“This is the systematic development of the mind. To me the very essence of education is concentration of mind, not the collecting of facts. If I had to do my education over again, and had any voice in the matter, I would not study facts at all. I would develop the power of concentration and detachment, and then with a perfect instrument I could collect facts at will. Side by side, in the child, should be developed the power of concentration and detachment.” [3]

I say more on this in [Vol 4, Writings: Prose, What We Believe in]; [Vol 5, Notes from Lectures and Discourses, The Goal and Methods of Realisation]; [Vol 4, Translation: Prose, Our Present Social Problems]; [Vol 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, Concentration]; [Vol 4, Translation: Prose, The Education That India Needs]; [Vol 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora, The Future of India].

question: Is Western education in India good?

result.text: I wrote in The Education That India Needs that the foreign educational institutions are simply to get a lot of useful, practical slaves for a little money — to turn out a host of clerks, postmasters, telegraph operators, and so on.[1] I pointed out in a lecture on Women of India that the foreign conqueror is not there to do good to us; he wants his money.[2] I stated in The Education That India Needs that the chief cause of India's ruin has been the monopolising of the whole education and intelligence of the land by a handful of men.[1] I remarked in a dialogue with Sharatchandra Chakravarty that only three or four per cent of the people in India are educated, and not even one per cent of the women.[3] I noted in a lecture on Women of India that the standard of education and civilisation is very high in England, which makes a great change.[4] I argued in The Education That India Needs that education must be spread among the masses for India to rise again.[1]

question: What can India give to the West?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but my teachings make it clear that India's greatest gift to the West is spirituality — the eternal truths that have shaped the soul of humanity for millennia. This spiritual knowledge, rooted in the Vedas and the Upanishads, teaches the unity of all life, the immortality of the soul, and the path of self-realisation through renunciation and devotion [1]. It is not a gift of conquest or force, but one of silent influence, like the dew that brings forth the bloom of roses [2]. India has always been the spiritual teacher of the world, and even now, as the West stands at a crossroads, it is India that must guide it with the light of its ancient wisdom. This is not merely a historical duty, but a divine necessity — for the West, in its search for meaning beyond materialism, will find in India the answers to the deepest questions of life [3]. Let this spiritual message of India be spread across the world, not as a relic of the past, but as a living force that can uplift and transform the hearts of men everywhere.

question: What do you think of Christ?

result.text: As I told the audience at Chicago, I believe in the crucifixion of Christ, though I rely on books for this knowledge, and I am aware that mere book testimony is rather shaky ground.[1] I argued in my lecture that the teachings of the Sermon on the Mount are a guide worth following, and that the words of Buddha, who lived five hundred years before Christ, were full of blessings.[1] In my lecture on discipleship, I criticized those who claim to believe in Christ without truly understanding him, calling them fit for a lunatic asylum.[2] I stated in my notes that the Trinitarian Christ is elevated above us, and the Unitarian Christ is merely a moral man, but neither can help us unless we see Christ as the Incarnation of God.[3] I emphasized in my lecture that the best commentary on the life of a great teacher is his own life, and that Christ's teachings should not be distorted to fit modern sensibilities.[4] I explained in my notes that Jesus Christ was God — the Personal God become man — and that we must worship the human manifestation of God as God.[5] I noted in my lecture that the wave of spiritual ideals rises and falls, but both are necessary, and that the same movement of succession is seen in all aspects of life.[6]

question: What can Hinduism learn from Islam?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but I can reason from my principles. Hinduism, with its infinite adaptability and inclusiveness, has much to learn from Islam's profound sense of unity and equality. Islam, as I have noted, approaches equality in a manner that is appreciable and commendable [1]. Its emphasis on the oneness of God and the brotherhood of all mankind offers a perspective that can deepen the spiritual unity within Hinduism. Furthermore, the practical and disciplined aspects of Islamic life may inspire Hinduism to strengthen its social and communal structures. Hinduism, as I have often said, is all-receptive and ever-willing to embrace the best of all traditions [2]. A junction of Hinduism and Islam—Vedanta brain and Islam body—may lead to a more harmonious and enlightened society [3]. Thus, in the spirit of mutual learning and growth, Hinduism can find much to admire and adopt from Islam.

question: Are the Vedas books?

result.text:
The Vedas are described as a vast collection of literature, similar to the Bible, but not a single book.
“There was already in India a vast religion with an organised scripture — the Vedas; and these Vedas existed as a mass of literature and not a book — just as you find the Old Testament, the Bible. Now, the Bible is a mass of literature of different ages; different persons are the writers, and so on. It is a collection.” [1]

The Vedas are so vast that if all the texts were brought together, they would not fit in a single room.
“They were so vast — the mass of writings — that if the texts alone were brought here, this room would not contain them.” [2]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Lectures and Discourses, The Vedanta Philosophy].

question: What is the Gita's central teaching?

result.text:
The Gita's central teaching is to remain calm and steadfast in all circumstances, with one's body, mind, and soul centred at God's Feet.
“Swamiji: Ay, that's it! Intense action in the whole body, and withal a face expressing the profound calmness and serenity of the blue sky. This is the central idea of the Gita — to be calm and steadfast in all circumstances, with one's body, mind, and soul centred at His hallowed Feet!” [1]

The Gita teaches that when we can get out of the narrow centre of the body, we shall realise God — our true Self.
“God is a circle whose circumference is nowhere and whose centre is everywhere, and when we can get out of the narrow centre of body, we shall realise God — our true Self.” [2]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Lectures and Discourses, The Gita I].

question: Did Krishna exist?

result.text: As I discussed in my lecture on the Gita, there is much doubt about the historical existence of Krishna, with many legends and stories having been attached to him over time.[1] I noted that in ancient times, there was little emphasis on historical research, and many stories about Krishna may have been invented or exaggerated.[1] I mentioned that Krishna is a central figure in the Gita, and while some believe he was a king, others think he may have been a spiritual teacher or a combination of both.[2] I pointed out that the stories of Krishna's life, like those of Jesus, have similarities, but also differences, and that these stories may have been shaped over time.[3] I suggested that Krishna may have been a real person, but that many of the stories surrounding him may have been added later, making it difficult to determine his true historical identity.[1] I acknowledged that some people believe Krishna was a great king who lived in ancient times, but that his life and teachings have been surrounded by many legends.[2] I explained that the historical accuracy of Krishna's life is difficult to verify due to the lack of reliable records from ancient times.[1]

question: Should one eat meat?

result.text:
I acknowledge that taking life is sinful, but I also recognize that meat-eating may be necessary in certain circumstances.
“The taking of life is undoubtedly sinful; but so long as vegetable food is not made suitable to the human system through progress in chemistry, there is no other alternative but meat-eating. So long as man shall have to live a Râjasika (active) life under circumstances like the present, there is no other way except through meat-eating. It is true that the Emperor Asoka saved the lives of millions of animals by the threat of the sword; but is not the slavery of a thousand years more dreadful than that?” [1]

question: How should India reform?

result.text: I did not speak to this directly, but my views on reform in India are grounded in the principle that true progress must come from within, rooted in the nation's own spiritual and cultural heritage [1]. India must not be forced into the mold of other nations; her reform must be a continuation of her past, guided by the wisdom of her own sages and the strength of her religious traditions [2]. Social reform is necessary, but it must not be imposed by external ideals or the tyranny of a minority; it must arise from the people themselves, through education and the awakening of their consciousness [3]. The reform of India lies in awakening the spiritual heart, in breaking through the inertia of centuries of servitude, and in moving forward along the path laid down by the sages, not by destroying what is good but by elevating it to higher truths [4]. India's strength is in her religion, and when that is made strong, all other aspects of life will follow in harmony.

question: Are you a political agitator?

result.text: I told Alasinga in a letter from the United States that I am no politician or political agitator, and that I care only for the Spirit.[1] In my lecture on My Plan of Campaign, I argued that in India, religious life is the centre of national vitality, and that throwing it off would lead to the nation's extinction.[2] I stated in a dialogue with Sharat Chandra Chakravarty that social reform must be preached by showing how much more spiritual a life the new system will bring.[3] In an interview, I was asked about social reform movements in America and England, but I emphasized that in India, religion is the one and only occupation of life.[4][5] In my lecture on the Address of Welcome Presented at Calcutta, I said that we must conquer the world by preaching the truths of our Shâstras, and that this will unite us as a race.[6] In my notes from Madras, I mentioned that there have been two lines of progress in the world — political and religious — and that the Hindus are everything in the latter.[7]

question: What is the goal of nature?

result.text:
The goal of nature, according to my teachings, is not freedom or knowledge, but the realization that the Purusha, or pure consciousness, is separate from and unchanging amidst the constant changes of nature.
“This is the real goal of practice — discrimination between the real and the unreal, knowing that the Purusha is not nature, that it is neither matter nor mind, and that because it is not nature, it cannot possibly change. It is only nature which changes, combining and re-combining, dissolving continually. When through constant practice we begin to discriminate, ignorance will vanish, and the Purusha will begin to shine in its real nature — omniscient, omnipotent, omnipresent.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 5, Notes from Lectures and Discourses, Law and Freedom].

question: Where is God?

result.text:
I believe that each of us is both personal and impersonal, and that our true nature is omnipresent.
“We are personalised impersonal beings. If you use the word in the absolute sense, we are impersonal; but if you use it in a relative meaning, we are personal.” [1]

You are everywhere, though you may only be conscious of being in one place at a time.
“You are omnipresent; only you have the consciousness of being concentrated in one point. That point has taken up particles of matter, and formed them into a machine to express itself.” [2]

question: What is the goal of life?

result.text:
The ultimate goal of life, according to my teachings, is re-union with God, or the realization of the divinity within every man.
“The ultimate goal of all mankind, the aim and end of all religions, is but one — re-union with God, or, what amounts to the same, with the divinity which is every man's true nature. But while the aim is one, the method of attaining may vary with the different temperaments of men.” [1]

The goal of the soul, as I have explained, is liberation — freedom from all limitations, and the realization of its infinite nature.
“There is one idea with all, and that is liberation. Man is infinite; and this limitation in which he exists now is not his nature. But through these limitations he is struggling upward and forward until he reaches the infinite, the unlimited, his birthright, his nature. All these combinations and recombinations and manifestations that we see round us are not the aim or the goal, but merely by the way and in passing. These combinations as earths and suns, and moons and stars, right and wrong, good and bad, our laughter and our tears, our joys and sorrows, are to enable us to gain experience through which the soul manifests its perfect nature and throws off limitation. No more, then, is it bound by laws either of internal or external nature. It has gone beyond all law, beyond all limitation, beyond all nature.” [2]

I say more on this in [Vol 3, Lectures and Discourses, Unity, the Goal of Religion].

question: Is man born a sinner?

result.text:
Nowhere is it said in the Vedas that man is born a sinner.
“Nowhere is it said in the Vedas that man is born a sinner. To say so is a great libel on human nature.” [1]

Be not deluded by your religion teaching original sin, for the same religion teaches original purity.
“"Be not deluded by your religion teaching original sin, for the same religion teaches original purity. When Adam fell, he fell from purity. (Applause) Purity is our real nature, and to regain that is the object of all religion. All men are pure; all men are good. Some objections can be raised to them, and you ask why some men are brutes? That man you call a brute is like the diamond in the dirt and dust — brush the dust off and it is a diamond, just as pure as if the dust had never been on it, and we must admit that every soul is a big diamond.” [2]

question: Do I need a teacher?

result.text:
Yes, you need a teacher, and it is important to understand that the true teacher is not merely a physical being, but a spiritual guide who can transmit knowledge and power in various ways.
“But first you must find a teacher, a true teacher, and you must remember that he is not just a man. You may get a teacher in the body; but the real teacher is not in the body; he is not the physical man — he is not as he appears to your eyes. It may be the teacher will come to you as a human being, and you will receive the power from him. Sometimes he will come in a dream and transmit things to the world. The power of the teacher may come to us in many ways. But for us ordinary mortals the teacher must come, and our preparation must go on till he comes.” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 3, Bhakti-Yoga, Ch. 5: Qualifications of the Aspirant and the Teacher].

question: Are miracles and psychic powers signs of holiness?

result.text:
I have seen that even demoniacal men can perform miracles, but they are not signs of holiness.
“But you must not mix up Christ or Buddha with hobgoblins flying through the air and all that sort of nonsense. Sacrilege! Christ coming into a spiritualistic seance to dance!” [1]

The true power of Christ lies not in miracles, but in the spiritual teachings and love that endure forever.
“The other is the spiritual power of Christ which will live and always has lived — an almighty, gigantic love, and the words of truth which He preached. The action of healing men at a glance is forgotten, but His saying, "Blessed are the pure in heart", that lives today. These words are a gigantic magazine of power — inexhaustible. So long as the human mind lasts, so long as the name of God is not forgotten, these words will roll on and on and never cease to be.” [2]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Preface]; [Vol 1, Raja-Yoga, Ch. 4: The Psychic Prana].

question: What are India's national ideals?

result.text:
India's national ideals are rooted in spirituality and renunciation, as I have emphasized throughout my teachings.
“The national ideals of India are RENUNCIATION and SERVICE. Intensify her in those channels, and the rest will take care of itself.” [1]

Religion, not politics or military power, is the backbone of India's national life.
“Not politics nor military power, not commercial supremacy nor mechanical genius furnishes India with that backbone, but religion; and religion alone is all that we have and mean to have. Spirituality has been always in India.” [2]

The great ideal of India is Brahminhood, which represents a spiritual and philosophical pursuit.
“The great ideal of India — Brahminhood.” [3]

Spirituality is the defining characteristic of Hinduism and the core of India's national identity.
“With the Hindus you will find one national idea — spirituality. In no other religion, in no other sacred books of the world, will you find so much energy spent in defining the idea of God.” [4]

The Indian ideal is not to attain heaven, but to transcend all worldly existence and achieve freedom.
“The Indian ideal is not to go to heaven. Get out of this earth, get out of hell, and get out of heaven!” [5]

I say more on this in [Vol 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora, Address of Welcome Presented at Calcutta and Reply]; [Vol 5, Interviews, India and England]; [Vol 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora, The Common Bases of Hinduism].

question: Is religion about doctrine?

result.text:
Religion is not about doctrine, but about realization and experience.
“The next idea that I want to bring to you is that religion does not consist in doctrines or dogmas. It is not what you read, nor what dogmas you believe that is of importance, but what you realise.” [1]

Religion is not a collection of frothy words or intellectual assent.
“We should get beyond the prattle of men who think that religion is merely a mass of frothy words, that it is only a system of doctrines; to whom religion is only a little intellectual assent or dissent; to whom religion is believing in certain words which their own priests tell them; to whom religion is something which their forefathers believed; to whom religion is a certain form of ideas and superstitions to which they cling because they are their national superstitions.” [2]

Too much doctrine can lead to evil and necessitate reformation.
“"When there is too much doctrine, too much belief in my father's religion, too much rational superstition, a change is needed.” [3]

Doctrine has nothing to do with salvation.
“With us doctrine has nothing whatever to do with salvation.” [4]

This is the whole of religion.
“This is the whole of religion.” [5]

Religion is a realization, not talk, not doctrines, nor theories.
“Religion is a realization, not talk, not doctrines, nor theories, however beautiful all these may be. Religion is being and becoming, not hearing or acknowledging.” [6]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Lectures and Discourses, Mohammed]; [Vol 9, Notes of Lectures and Classes, The Gita — III]; [Vol 2, Reports in American Newspapers, Less Doctrine and More Bread]; [Vol 7, Inspired Talks, Sunday, July 14, 1895].

question: Who was your Master?

result.text: My Master was Ramakrishna Paramahamsa.[1][2][3][4][5][6][7] He was a great Indian sage, deeply imbued with the spirit of the Vedanta philosophy.[3] He was born in the Hooghly district in 1836 and died in 1886.[3] He was not a very learned man, but a very holy one.[3] He produced a deep effect on the life of Keshab Chandra Sen and others.[3] He obtained a wonderful insight into the spiritual world through discipline of the body and subduing of the mind.[3] His face was distinguished by a childlike tenderness, profound humility, and remarkable sweetness of expression.[3] He refused to think of body and illness, as his mind was continually conscious of God.[5] In his Master, Ramakrishna Paramahamsa, I found the key to life.[7]

question: Should the masses learn Sanskrit?

result.text:
I believe that the masses should learn Sanskrit, as it is the key to raising their condition and achieving true cultural and educational empowerment.
“The only safety, I tell you men who belong to the lower castes, the only way to raise your condition is to study Sanskrit, and this fighting and writing and frothing against the higher castes is in vain, it does no good, and it creates fight and quarrel, and this race, unfortunately already divided, is going to be divided more and more. The only way to bring about the levelling of caste is to appropriate the culture, the education which is the strength of the higher castes. That done, you have what you want” [1]

I say more on this in [Vol 1, Addresses at the Parliament of Religions, Buddhism, the Fulfilment of Hinduism].

question: Who should decide women's development?

result.text:
I believe that women should be given the opportunity to solve their own problems in their own way.
“"By no means," said the Swami, "but our right of interference is limited entirely to giving education. Women must be put in a position to solve their own problems in their own way. No one can or ought to do this for them. And our Indian women are as capable of doing it as any in the world."” [1]

Educating women first and allowing them to take charge of their own development is essential.
“Educate your women first and leave them to themselves; then they will tell you what reforms are necessary for them. In matters concerning them, who are you?” [2]

I say more on this in [Vol 9, Lectures and Discourses, The Women of India]; [Vol 9, Excerpts from Sister Nivedita's Book, Walks and Talks Beside the Jhelum].
